sanskrit_sloka:
ధృతరాష్ట్ర ఉవాచ ।
ధర్మ క్షేత్రే కురుక్షేత్రే సమవేతా యుయుత్సవః ।
మామకాః పాండవాశ్చైవ కిమకుర్వత సంజయ ।। 1 ।।
translation_en: Dhritarashtra said: O Sanjaya, what did my sons and Pandu's sons do, assembled in Kurukshetra, the land of Dharma?
explanation_en: Dhritarashtra opens with a question that reveals everything about his character: he knows something terrible is about to happen, but he's choosing to ask about it rather than prevent it. The blind king's anxiety isn't about peace — it's about which side will win. He's not a neutral observer; he's a father gambling with his children's lives. His question to Sanjaya isn't curiosity — it's the beginning of his attempt to control a narrative he can no longer influence. This is what moral blindness looks like: seeing clearly enough to worry, but not clearly enough to act.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Dhritarashtra Uvacha — Dhritarashtra Palikenu; dharma kshetre — the land of dharma; kuru-kshetre — at Kurukshetra; samavetah  — involved; yuyutsavah — with a desire for war; mamakah — my sons; Pandava — the sons of Pandu; Cha — and; eva — truly; kim — what; akurvata — did; Sanjaya — O Sanjaya.

sanskrit_sloka:
సంజయ ఉవాచ ।
దృష్ట్వా తు పాండవానీకం వ్యూఢం దుర్యోధనస్తదా ।
ఆచార్యముపసంగమ్య రాజా వచనమబ్రవీత్ ।। 2 ।।
translation_en: Sanjayu Palikenu: Duryodhana, seeing the Pandava army stationed in military strategy, approached his teacher Dronacharya and said this.
explanation_en: Duryodhana doesn't approach Drona for advice — he approaches him for reassurance. He's already made his decision to fight; now he needs his teacher to validate it. The way he describes the Pandava army as 'strategically arranged' shows he's already thinking in terms of tactical advantage, not moral rightness. He's not asking 'should we fight?' but 'how do we win?' This is the mind of someone who has already crossed the line and is now looking for allies in his delusion.

sanskrit_sloka:
పశ్యైతాం పాండుపుత్రాణామ్ ఆచార్య మహతీం చమూమ్ ।
వ్యూఢాం ద్రుపదపుత్రేణ తవ శిష్యేణ ధీమతా ।। 3 ।।
translation_en: Duryodhana spoke:  Respected Guruvarya! Behold this great army of Pandavas, most strategically held by your dear disciple, the son of Drupada.
explanation_en: The bitter irony of Duryodhana's words isn't lost on him: he's pointing out that Drona's own student, Drishtadyumna, now commands the army against them. He's using guilt as a weapon, reminding his teacher that his generosity has produced a formidable enemy. This is manipulation dressed as observation — Duryodhana knows exactly what he's doing. He's not just reporting facts; he's making Drona complicit in what comes next.
word_by_word_meaning_en: pasya — see; etham — of this; pandu-putranam — the sons of King Pandu; Acharya — Guruvarya; mahatim — great; chamoom — the army; Vyuham —  a military strategic hold; drupada-putrena — Drishtadyumna, the son of Drupada; tava — of you; sisyena — the disciple; dhi-mata — intelligent.

sanskrit_sloka:
['అత్ర శూరా మహేష్వాసా భీమార్జునసమా యుధి ।
యుయుధానో విరాటశ్చ ద్రుపదశ్చ మహారథః ।। 4 ।।', 'ధృష్టకేతుశ్చేకితానః కాశీరాజశ్చ వీర్యవాన్ ।
పురుజిత్ కుంతిభోజశ్చ శైబ్యశ్చ నరపుంగవః ।। 5 ।।', 'యుధామన్యుశ్చ విక్రాంత ఉత్తమౌజాశ్చ వీర్యవాన్ ।
సౌభద్రో ద్రౌపదేయాశ్చ సర్వ ఏవ మహారథాః ।। 6 ।।']
translation_en: Look at the many mighty warriors in the army on their side - like Yuudhana, Virata and Drupada who wear great bows and are equal to Bhimarjuna. There were the mighty Dhrishtaketa, Chekita, the heroic Kasiraja, Purujittu, Kuntibhoja and Saibya - all of them the best of men. As in their army - the brave Yudhamanya, the heroic Uttamauja, the son of Subhadra, the sons of Draupadi - all these were warriors.
explanation_en: Duryodhana lists the Pandava warriors with the precision of someone who has been studying them closely. He knows their names, their strengths, their capabilities. This isn't casual observation — it's the catalog of a man who has been planning for this moment. By naming each warrior individually, he transforms them from abstract threats into specific problems to be solved. The detail reveals his anxiety: he's not confident in victory, he's trying to convince himself it's possible.

['అత్ర శూరా మహేష్వాసా భీమార్జునసమా యుధి ।
యుయుధానో విరాటశ్చ ద్రుపదశ్చ మహారథః ।। 4 ।।', 'ధృష్టకేతుశ్చేకితానః కాశీరాజశ్చ వీర్యవాన్ ।
పురుజిత్ కుంతిభోజశ్చ శైబ్యశ్చ నరపుంగవః ।। 5 ।।', 'యుధామన్యుశ్చ విక్రాంత ఉత్తమౌజాశ్చ వీర్యవాన్ ।
సౌభద్రో ద్రౌపదేయాశ్చ సర్వ ఏవ మహారథాః ।। 6 ।।']
translation_en: Look at the many mighty warriors in the army on their side - like Yuudhana, Virata and Drupada who wear great bows and are equal to Bhimarjuna. There were the mighty Dhrishtaketa, Chekita, the heroic Kasiraja, Purujittu, Kuntibhoja and Saibya - all of them the best of men. As in their army - the brave Yudhamanya, the heroic Uttamauja, the son of Subhadra, the sons of Draupadi - all these were warriors.
explanation_en: The phrase 'best of men' used to describe enemy warriors reveals Duryodhana's grudging respect for their abilities. He's not underestimating his opponents — he's acknowledging their strength while preparing to fight them. This is more honest than blind confidence, but it's still a form of denial: recognizing the threat doesn't make it less dangerous. His detailed assessment shows he takes the threat seriously, but his conclusion — we must fight anyway — shows he's trapped in a logic of his own making.

['అత్ర శూరా మహేష్వాసా భీమార్జునసమా యుధి ।
యుయుధానో విరాటశ్చ ద్రుపదశ్చ మహారథః ।। 4 ।।', 'ధృష్టకేతుశ్చేకితానః కాశీరాజశ్చ వీర్యవాన్ ।
పురుజిత్ కుంతిభోజశ్చ శైబ్యశ్చ నరపుంగవః ।। 5 ।।', 'యుధామన్యుశ్చ విక్రాంత ఉత్తమౌజాశ్చ వీర్యవాన్ ।
సౌభద్రో ద్రౌపదేయాశ్చ సర్వ ఏవ మహారథాః ।। 6 ।।']
translation_en: Look at the many mighty warriors in the army on their side - like Yuudhana, Virata and Drupada who wear great bows and are equal to Bhimarjuna. There were the mighty Dhrishtaketa, Chekita, the heroic Kasiraja, Purujittu, Kuntibhoja and Saibya - all of them the best of men. As in their army - the brave Yudhamanya, the heroic Uttamauja, the son of Subhadra, the sons of Draupadi - all these were warriors.
explanation_en: The inclusion of the younger generation — Abhimanyu, Draupadi's sons — adds a layer of tragedy to Duryodhana's catalog. These young men are being drawn into a conflict they didn't create, and Duryodhana is listing them as assets to be deployed. He's not just counting warriors; he's counting lives that will be lost. The comprehensive nature of his assessment shows he understands the scope of what's about to happen, but his determination remains unshaken.

sanskrit_sloka:
అస్మాకం తు విశిష్టా యే తాన్నిబోధ ద్విజోత్తమ ।
నాయకా మమ సైన్యస్య సంజ్ఞార్థం తాన్ బ్రవీమి తే ।। 7 ।।
translation_en: O Brahmin, hear also of the chief warriors on our side, who are most worthy of leaders. I am telling you about them now for your interest.
explanation_en: When Duryodhana shifts to his own army, the tone changes from anxiety to forced confidence. He's not reporting strengths — he's trying to build morale, starting with his own. The phrase 'for your interest' carries an undertone of manipulation: he's essentially saying these are the warriors whose fate depends on your performance. This is a leader who knows his side is outmatched and is trying to compensate with rhetoric.

sanskrit_sloka:
భవాన్ భీష్మశ్చ కర్ణశ్చ కృపశ్చ సమితింజయః ।
అశ్వత్థామా వికర్ణశ్చ సౌమదత్తిస్తథైవ చ ।। 8 ।।
translation_en: You, Bhishma, Karna, Kripacharya, Ashwatthama, Vikarna and Bhurishrava - all of them are ever victorious in battle.
explanation_en: Duryodhana names his greatest warriors with the pride of someone who believes names equal power. Bhishma, Karna, Kripacharya — these are legendary figures, but he's listing them like weapons in an arsenal. The description 'ever victorious in battle' is meant to be reassuring, but it's actually a reminder that victory is never guaranteed. His pride in these warriors masks his fear that even their combined strength might not be enough.

sanskrit_sloka:
అన్యే చ బహవః శూరా మదర్థే త్యక్తజీవితాః ।
నానాశస్త్ర ప్రహరణాః సర్వే యుద్ధవిశారదాః ।। 9 ।।
translation_en: Many more warriors are ready to lay down their lives for me. Armed with many weapons, all of them are proficient in martial arts.
explanation_en: The phrase 'ready to lay down their lives' reveals the depth of loyalty Duryodhana commands — but also the depth of his manipulation. He's not just describing willing soldiers; he's describing men who believe in his cause enough to die for it. The mention of diverse weaponry and martial expertise shows this is a professional army, not a militia. But the underlying message is clear: these men will die for you, so you better make sure it's worth it.
word_by_word_meaning_en: anye — others; cha — also; bahavah — many; Shurah — valiant warriors; madarthe — for me; tyakta-jivitah — ready to sacrifice; nana-sastra praharanah — one who has many weapons; Survey — All; Yuddha-visharadah — experts in the field of war.

sanskrit_sloka:
అపర్యాప్తం తదస్మాకం బలం భీష్మాభిరక్షితం।
పర్యాప్తం త్విదమేతేషాం బలం భీమాభిరక్షితం ।। 10 ।।
translation_en: Our military strength is unlimited and we are protected by father Bhishma, but the Pandava army protected by Bhima is limited.
explanation_en: Duryodhana's claim that his army's strength is 'unlimited' under Bhishma's protection is the kind of boast that reveals doubt. If he truly believed in inevitable victory, he wouldn't need to say it. The contrast between 'unlimited strength' and 'limited strength' is meant to create confidence, but it actually exposes his anxiety. He's not stating facts; he's trying to convince himself.
word_by_word_meaning_en: aparyaptam — limitless; tat — that; asmakam — of us; strength — strength; bhishma — by Bhishma's father; abhirashitam— being safely guarded; paripatam— limited; tu — but; Itam — this; etesham — of them; strength — strength; Bhima — Bhima; Abhirakshitam — carefully guarded.

sanskrit_sloka:
అయనేషు చ సర్వేషు యథాభాగమవస్థితాః ।
భీష్మమేవాభిరక్షంతు భవంతః సర్వ ఏవ హి ।। 11 ।।
translation_en: Therefore, I call upon all Kaurava Sena leaders to protect your strategic positions and render full cooperation to Bhishma Pitamahu.
explanation_en: Duryodhana's command to protect Bhishma's positions shows his understanding that morale matters as much as muscle. He's not just giving tactical orders; he's establishing the chain of command that will govern the Kaurava side. The instruction to 'give full support' reveals his recognition that individual strength means nothing without coordination. This is the transition from assessment to action — the moment when planning becomes preparation for war.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Ayaneshu — in strategic positions; Cha — and; Sarveshu — all; Yathabhaga — in your positions; avasthitah — remain; Bhishma — the father of Bhishma; eva — only; abhirakshanta — protect; bhavantah  — you; Survey — All; What hi — also.

sanskrit_sloka:
తస్య సంజనయన్ హర్షం కురువృద్ధః పితామహః ।
సింహనాదం వినద్యోచ్చైః శంఖం దధ్మౌ ప్రతాపవాన్ ।। 12 ।।
translation_en: Then Bhishma, the great progenitor of the Kuru clan, roared like a lion and filled his conch with a loud noise; This made Duryodhana happy.
explanation_en: Bhishma's lion-like roar isn't just a war cry — it's a statement of identity. The aged warrior is declaring that age hasn't diminished his spirit. His conch blast serves simultaneously as a challenge to the enemy and a reassurance to his own troops. This display of martial spirit visibly boosts Duryodhana's confidence, showing how much the Kaurava side depends on Bhishma's presence. The grandsire's roar is the sound of tradition meeting necessity.
word_by_word_meaning_en: tasya — to him; sanjanayan — cause; harsham — happiness; kuruvriddhah — an old man (Bhishma) of the Kuru clan; pitamahah — grandfather; simha-nadam — the lion's roar; vinadya — made noise; uchchaih — with a loud voice; sankham — the conch; dadhmau — rang out; pratapa-van — radiant.

sanskrit_sloka:
తతః శంఖాశ్చ భేర్యశ్చ పణవానకగోముఖాః ।
సహసైవాభ్యహన్యంత స శబ్దస్తుములోఽభవత్ ।। 13 ।।
translation_en: After that conches, drums, tambourines, bheris and horn instruments sounded at once, the sound of all of them together was terrifying.
explanation_en: The combined sound of conches, drums, and war instruments creates a sensory overload that mirrors the emotional turmoil about to unfold. This isn't just noise — it's the sound of two armies converting their fear into aggression. The terrible cacophony serves both to intimidate the enemy and steel one's own troops. But underneath the noise is the reality: these instruments of war will soon be creating real destruction, not just terrifying sounds.
word_by_word_meaning_en: tatah — after that; sankhah — conch shells; Cha — and; bheryah — the Bheris; Cha — and; panava-anaka — drums; go-mukah — horn instruments ; sahasa — all of a sudden; eva — indeed; abhyahanyanta — loud noises; sah — of that; shabdah — sound; tumulah — fearfully; abhavat — was.

sanskrit_sloka:
తతః శ్వేతైర్హయైర్యుక్తే మహతి స్యందనే స్థితౌ ।
మాధవః పాండవశ్చైవ దివ్యౌ శంఖౌ ప్రదధ్మతుః ।। 14 ।।
translation_en: Then, from the midst of the Pandava army, seated in a splendid chariot full of white horses, Madhava and Arjuna filled their divine conchshells.
explanation_en: Krishna's participation as charioteer rather than combatant establishes his unique role from the very beginning. He's not fighting alongside Arjuna; he's guiding him. The white horses symbolize purity in contrast to the aggression emanating from the opposing side. This reciprocal blast of conches represents the formal declaration that battle is about to commence — but it's also the beginning of a relationship that will transform Arjuna's understanding of duty.
word_by_word_meaning_en: tatah — after that; svetaih — white; hayaih — horses; yukte— tied; mahati — the great maina; syandane — the chariot; sthitau — sitting; Madhavah — Sri Krishna (husband of Goddess Lakshmi, goddess of auspiciousness); pandavah — Arjuna; Cha — and; eva — also; divyau — divine; Shankhau — the conch shells; pradhmatuh — filled.

sanskrit_sloka:
పాంచజన్యం హృషీకేశో దేవదత్తం ధనంజయః ।
పౌండ్రం దధ్మౌ మహాశంఖం భీమకర్మా వృకోదరః ।। 15 ।।
translation_en: Hrishikesh filled the conch known as 'Panchajanyam'. Arjuna fills Devadatta. A great eater and a doer of the most difficult tasks, Bhima filled a gigantic conch called 'Poundram'.
explanation_en: Each Pandava warrior's conch shell becomes an expression of personality and determination. Krishna's Panchajanya represents divine authority, Arjuna's Devadatta signals readiness for righteous fight, Bhima's massive Paundra reflects his enormous physical strength. These aren't just instruments — they're declarations of identity. The variety of sounds represents the diverse forces united under a common cause.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Panchajanyam — the conch named Panchajanyam; hrshika-esah — Sri Krishna (master of mind, senses); Devadatta — the conch named Devadatta; dhanam-jayah — Arjuna, conqueror of money; poundram — a conch named poundram; dadhmau — filled; mahasankha — a gigantic conch; bhima-karma — doing the most difficult tasks; Vrika-udarah — Bhima (the great eater).

sanskrit_sloka:
['అనంతవిజయం రాజా కుంతీపుత్రో యుధిష్ఠిరః ।
నకులః సహదేవశ్చ సుఘోషమణిపుష్పకౌ ।। 16 ।।', 'కాశ్యశ్చ పరమేష్వాసః శిఖండీ చ మహారథః ।
ధృష్టద్యుమ్నో విరాటశ్చ సాత్యకిశ్చాపరాజితః ।। 17 ।।', 'ద్రుపదో ద్రౌపదేయాశ్చ సర్వశః పృథివీపతే ।
సౌభద్రశ్చ మహాబాహుః శంఖాన్ దధ్ముః పృథక్ పృథక్ ।। 18 ।।']
translation_en: Oh ruler of the earth! Maharaja Yudhishthira completed Anantavijaya. Nakula Sahadeva, Sughosha filled the manipushpakams. The five sons of the great archer King Kasi, the charioteer Sikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, the invincible Satyaki, Drupada, and Draupadi; Strong-armed, Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra, all filled their conch shells.
explanation_en: The enumeration of Pandava conch blowers continues with Yudhishthira's Anantavijaya representing his endless virtue and authority. The mention of warriors from various kingdoms demonstrates the breadth of the Pandava alliance network. This comprehensive listing mirrors Duryodhana's earlier catalog but from the perspective of the forces of dharma. The variety of conch shells represents the diverse forces united for a common cause.

explanation_en: The narrative continues describing additional Pandava warriors sounding their conch shells in response to the Kaurava challenge. Each warrior's contribution adds to the mounting tension as both sides complete their preparations for imminent combat. The description of specific commanders and their distinctive instruments personalizes the approaching conflict. This extended passage of war preparations builds dramatic tension before the focus shifts to Arjuna's emotional crisis.

The five sons of the great archer King Kasi, the charioteer Sikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, the invincible Satyaki, Drupada, and Draupadi; Strong-armed, Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra, all filled their conch shells.
explanation_en: The final portion of the Pandava war cry description names the remaining commanders and their conch shells, completing the symphony of preparation. The comprehensive listing establishes that every significant warrior on the Pandava side has answered the call to battle. This thoroughness in documenting the war preparations reflects the gravity of the即将发生的 conflict. The accumulation of these details creates a sense of inevitability about the coming violence.

sanskrit_sloka:
స ఘోషో ధార్తరాష్ట్రాణాం హృదయాని వ్యదారయత్ ।
నభశ్చ పృథివీం చైవ తుములో ఽభ్యనునాదయన్ ।। 19 ।।
translation_en: O Dhritarashtra, the earth and heavens trembled at that terrible sound; It broke the hearts of your sons.
explanation_en: The combined sound of both armies' instruments shaking the earth and sky suggests that the即将发生的 violence offends the natural order itself. This cosmic reaction to the war preparations isn't just dramatic description — it's a statement about the moral weight of the conflict. The trembling of heaven and earth symbolizes the disruption of natural harmony that war represents. The specific mention of terror in the Kaurava ranks reveals that even their own war preparations frighten them.
word_by_word_meaning_en: sah — atty; ghoshah — noise; dhartarashtranam — of the sons of Dhritarashtra; hrudayani — hearts; vyadarayat — did the braddas; nabhah — sky; Cha — and; prithivim — earth; Cha — and; eva — truly; tumulo — a terrible sound; Abhyanunadayan — Resonate.

sanskrit_sloka:
అథ వ్యవస్థితాన్ దృష్ట్వా ధార్తరాష్ట్రాన్ కపిధ్వజః ।
ప్రవృత్తే శస్త్రసంపాతే ధనురుద్యమ్య పాండవః ।। 20 ।।
హృషీకేశం తదా వాక్యం ఇదమాహ మహీపతే ।
translation_en: At that time, Arjuna, the son of Pandu, who had the symbol of Hanuman on his chariot flag, took his bow. Seeing your sons standing in front of Samara, O king, Arjuna said to Sri Krishna.
explanation_en: Arjuna picking up his bow bearing Hanuman's emblem symbolizes strength and devotion — qualities he'll need in abundance. However, upon seeing the assembled Kaurava forces, he turns to Krishna with a request that signals his emerging doubt. This moment captures the precise instant when martial determination begins to crack under the weight of moral awareness. The flag of Hanuman fluttering above represents the divine protection that will guide Arjuna through his coming crisis.
word_by_word_meaning_en: atha — after; Systitan — Steady standing; drishtva  — seeing; Dhartarashtra — sons of Dhritarashtra; Kapi-dhvajah — met the vanara (monkey) on the flag; Pravrutte — ready to start; sastra sampathe — to use weapons; Dhanuh — the bow (bow); குத்திய்யு   — to lift up; Pandavah — Arjuna, son of Pandu; Hrishikesam — with Sri Krishna; tada  — then; Sentence — words; Itam — these; Aha — to speak; Mahi-pathe — the king.

sanskrit_sloka: ['అర్జున ఉవాచ ।\nసెనయోరుభయోర్మధ్యే రథం స్థాపయ మేఽచ్యుత ।। 21 ।।', 'యావదేతాన్ నిరీక్షేఽహం యోద్దుకామానవస్థితాన్ ।\nకైర్మయా సహ యోద్ధవ్యమ్ అస్మిన్ రణసముద్యమే ।। 22 ।।']
translation_en: Arjuna said this. Achyuta (Sri Krishna), please stop my chariot between the two armies. In this great struggle, I must test who is standing on the battlefield and who is to fight.
explanation_en: Arjuna's request to position the chariot between the armies reveals his desire to fully comprehend the situation before committing to violence. He's not asking for tactical advantage — he's asking for clarity. The phrase 'test who is standing' suggests he needs to identify specific individuals rather than face an anonymous enemy. This strategic pause shows Arjuna's thoughtful nature contrasting with the冲动 of his cousins.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Arjuna Uvacha — Arjuna spoke; senayoh — the armies; ubhayoh — two; madhe  — in the middle; ratham — the chariot; sthāthāya — put down; May — of me; Achyuta — Sri Krishna (who is without any faults); All — to what extent; Ethan  — of this; nirikshe — seeing; Aham — I; yoddu-kaman  — for war; avasthithan — standing still; kaih  — with whom; maya  — with me; co — together; yoddhavyam  — to fight; Asmin — of this; Rana Samudyame — in the great struggle.

sanskrit_sloka: ['అర్జున ఉవాచ ।\nసెనయోరుభయోర్మధ్యే రథం స్థాపయ మేఽచ్యుత ।। 21 ।।', 'యావదేతాన్ నిరీక్షేఽహం యోద్దుకామానవస్థితాన్ ।\nకైర్మయా సహ యోద్ధవ్యమ్ అస్మిన్ రణసముద్యమే ।। 22 ।।']
translation_en: Arjuna said this. Achyuta (Sri Krishna), please stop my chariot between the two armies. In this great struggle, I must test who is standing on the battlefield and who is to fight.
explanation_en: The repetition of Arjuna's request emphasizes his urgent need to see clearly before taking any irreversible action. He's not being indecisive — he's being careful. The phrase 'in this great struggle' acknowledges the magnitude of the conflict while the desire to test indicates his need for personal assessment. This moment of hesitation before battle represents a universal human experience of seeking clarity before making consequential decisions.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Arjuna Uvacha — Arjuna spoke; senayoh — the armies; ubhayoh — two; madhe  — in the middle; ratham — the chariot; sthāthāya — put down; May — of me; Achyuta — Sri Krishna (who is without any faults); All — to what extent; Ethan  — of this; nirikshe — seeing; Aham — I; yoddu-kaman  — for war; avasthithan — standing still; kaih  — with whom; maya  — with me; co — together; yoddhavyam  — to fight; Asmin — of this; Rana Samudyame — in the great struggle.

sanskrit_sloka:
యోత్స్యమానాన వేక్షేఽహం య ఏతేఽత్ర సమాగతాః ।
ధార్తరాష్ట్రస్య దుర్బుద్దేః యుద్దే ప్రియచికీర్షవః ।। 23 ।।
translation_en: I want to see all those who have come to war on his side to please the mischievous Dhritarashtra's son.
explanation_en: Arjuna's desire to see all those gathered to fight 'to please the mischievous son' reveals his view that this war serves only Duryodhana's selfish ambitions. He's not just identifying enemies — he's identifying victims of someone else's greed. By wanting to recognize each warrior, he acknowledges their individual humanity rather than seeing them as faceless enemies to be destroyed. This desire for recognition reflects his growing awareness that he will be fighting people he knows and respects.
word_by_word_meaning_en: yotsyamanan  — those who come to war; avekshe aham — I want to see;ye — who; Athe  — they; Atra  — here; samagatah — composed; dhartarashtrasya — to the son of Dhritarashtra; durbuddeh — having a dull mind; yudde — in the war; priya-chikirshavah — to please.

sanskrit_sloka:
సంజయ ఉవాచ ।
ఏవముక్తో హృషీకేశో గుడాకేశేన భారత ।
సేనయోరుభయోర్మధ్యే స్థాపయిత్వా రథోత్తమమ్ ।। 24 ।।
translation_en: Sanjaya said: O Dhritarashtra, thus, as requested by Arjuna, conqueror of sleep, Sri Krishna drove that glorious chariot between the two armies.
explanation_en: Sanjaya's description of Arjuna as 'conqueror of sleep' — one who has overcome spiritual ignorance through his quest for knowledge — creates an ironic contrast with his current state of confusion. The physical positioning between opposing forces creates a dramatic tableau where the entire conflict can be surveyed from a single vantage point. The glory of the chariot represents the divine vehicle through which spiritual wisdom will be transmitted to the confused warrior.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Sanjaya Uwacha — Sanjaya said; evam — in this way; uktah  — said; Hrishikesah — Sri Krishna (Lord of the senses); Gudakesena — by Arjuna (by the conqueror of sleep); Bharata — descendant of Bharata; senayoh — armies; ubhayoh — two; madhe  — in the middle; Establishment — stop; ratha-uttamam — the best chariot.

sanskrit_sloka:
భీష్మద్రోణప్రముఖతః సర్వేషాం చ మహీక్షితామ్ ।
ఉవాచ పార్థ పశ్యైతాన్ సమవేతాన్ కురూనితి ।। 25 ।।
translation_en: In the presence of Bhishma, Dronacharya and other kings, Lord Krishna said, "O Partha, see the Kurus clan gathered here".
explanation_en: Krishna's instruction to 'see' is both literal and metaphorical — urging Arjuna to look beyond表面现象 to understand the deeper truth of the situation. The presence of Bhishma, Dronacharya, and other kings represents the entire social and family structure that the war will destroy. This moment of collective viewing establishes the scope of what is at stake in the coming conflict. Krishna's guidance as charioteer foreshadows his role as spiritual teacher in the chapters to come.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Bhishma — Father Bhishma; Drona — Dronacharya; வெரைத்து  — in the presence of; Sarvesham — All; Cha — and; mahi-kshitam — other kings; Uwacha — Palikenu; Partha — Arjuna  (son of Pritha); pasya — see; Ethan  — of this; samavetan — joining; Kuroon — Descendants of Kuru; iti — in this way.

sanskrit_sloka:
తత్రాపశ్యత్ స్థితాన్ పార్థః పిత్రూ నథ పితామహాన్ ।
ఆచార్యాన్మాతులాన్భ్రాతూన్ పుత్రాన్ పౌత్రాన్ సఖీం స్తథా ।। 26 ।।
శ్వశురాన్ సుహృదశ్చైవ సేనాయోరుభయోరపి ।
translation_en: There Arjuna saw his fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, cousins, sons, grandsons, friends, uncles and well-wishers who were in both armies.
explanation_en: Arjuna's recognition of his fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, cousins, sons, and friends arrayed on both sides transforms an abstract military conflict into a personal tragedy of devastating proportions. The comprehensive listing of familial relationships reveals the intimate nature of this civil war where family fights against family. The inclusion of well-wishers and friends among the enemy forces compounds the moral impossibility of the situation.
word_by_word_meaning_en: tatra — there; apasyat — saw; sthithan — standing; parthah — Arjuna; Pithrun — fathers (step-fathers, grandfathers); atha — after; pitamahan — grandfathers; acharyaan — teachers; matulan — uncles; bhratrin — brothers; putran — the sons; poutran — grandchildren; sakheen — friends; tatha — yet ; svashuran — (child-giving) uncles; suhridah —well-wishers; Cha — and; eva — truly; Senayoh — the armies; ubhayoh — in both; Api — also.

sanskrit_sloka:
తాన్ సమీక్ష్య స కౌంతేయః సర్వాన్ బంధూనవస్థితాన్ ।। 27 ।।
కృపయా పరయావిష్టో విషీదన్నిదమబ్రవీత్ ।
translation_en: Arjuna, the son of Kunti, seeing all his relatives there, filled with compassion, uttered this in great sorrow.
explanation_en: Arjuna's deep compassion upon seeing all his relatives gathered for mutual destruction reveals that his emotional response stems from love and empathy rather than from fear or cowardice. This spontaneous outpouring of grief marks the beginning of the great philosophical dialogue that will form the rest of the Bhagavad Gita. His sorrow represents the natural human response to the prospect of harming those one loves deeply.
word_by_word_meaning_en: tan — these; முக்க்குயுக்கு — seen pidapa; sah — they; kaunteyah — Arjuna; Son of Kunti; Sarvan — all; bandhun — relatives; avasthithan — as it were; kripaya — with compassion; paraya — much; avishtaḥ — being composed; vishidan — great sadness; Itam — thus; Abraveit — Palikenu.

sanskrit_sloka:
అర్జున ఉవాచ ।
దృష్ట్వేమం స్వజనం కృష్ణ యుయుత్సుం సముపస్థితమ్ ।। 28 ।।
సీదంతి మమ గాత్రాణి ముఖం చ పరిశుష్యతి ।
translation_en: Arjuna said: O Krishna, seeing my relatives ready for battle and trying to kill each other, my limbs fail and my mouth dries up.
explanation_en: Arjuna's physical and mental collapse — drying mouth, failing limbs, trembling, disorientation — represents the body's involuntary rejection of the impending violence. This isn't mere nervousness; it's a profound spiritual crisis that affects his entire being. The description of physical symptoms reveals how deeply the moral conflict has penetrated his consciousness. This visceral reaction demonstrates that Arjuna's objection to war is not intellectual but comes from the deepest part of his soul.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Arjuna Uvacha — Arjuna said; drishtva — after seeing; Imam  — of this; sva-janam — relatives (own); Krishna — Krishna; yuutsum — with zeal for battle; samupasthitam — included; sidanti — trembling; mama — of me; Gatrani  — (body) limbs; face — mouth; Cha — and; Parishushyati — does not dry up.

sanskrit_sloka: ['వేపథుశ్చ శరీరే మే రోమహర్షశ్చ జాయతే ।। 29 ।।', 'గాండీవం స్రంసతే హస్తాత్ త్వక్చైవ పరిదహ్యతే ।\nన చ శక్నోమ్యవస్థాతుం భ్రమతీవ చ మే మనః ।। 30 ।।', 'నిమిత్తాని చ పశ్యామి విపరీతాని కేశవ ।\nన చ శ్రేయోఽనుపశ్యామి హత్వా స్వజనమాహవే \xa0।। 31 ।।']
translation_en: My whole body was shaking; Hair is getting thick.  My bow, the gandivam, slips away and all my skin is missing. My mind is wandering in a state of confusion. I can't hold myself steady anymore. O Krishna, slayer of the demon Kesi (Kesavah), there are ominous omens everywhere. Killing one's own kinsmen in this war, I fail to see how any good can come of it.
explanation_en: Arjuna's hair standing on end and his bow slipping from his grasp show the complete overwhelming nature of his moral crisis. The loss of control over his body and mind shows this is not a strategic retreat but a genuine spiritual and emotional breakdown. His skin burning and mind reeling represent the torment of one who sees no righteous path forward through the situation. The repeated address to Krishna as 'slayer of the demon Kesi' appeals for divine intervention in this seemingly impossible situation.

Killing one's own kinsmen in this war, I fail to see how any good can come of it.
explanation_en: Arjuna's physical distress intensifying — mind wandering in confusion, inability to maintain composure — shows that his moral objection has completely paralyzed his warrior identity and training. His body rebels against the command to fight even as his social duty and training demand it. This complete systems failure represents the moment when human conscience overrides conditioned behavior and social expectation.

explanation_en: Arjuna's question about the purpose of fighting when killing his own kinsmen would bring only sorrow strikes at the heart of all worldly ambition. His observation that he sees only evil consequences in killing family members shows his moral clarity despite the emotional turmoil consuming him. This verse captures the universal human realization that worldly success means nothing if achieved through the destruction of human relationships.

sanskrit_sloka: ['న కాంక్షే విజయం కృష్ణ న చ రాజ్యం సుఖాని చ ।\nకిం నో రాజ్యేన గోవింద కిం భోగైర్జీవితేన వా ।। 32 ।।', 'యేషామర్థే కాంక్షితం నో రాజ్యం భోగాః సుఖాని చ ।\nత ఇమేఽవస్థితా యుద్ధే ప్రాణాంస్త్యక్త్వా ధనాని చ ।। 33 ।।']
translation_en: O Krishna, I do not want victory, kingdom, or the happiness that comes from them. What is the use of the kingdom, of the pleasures, of this life, when those for whom we want all this are fighting against us?
explanation_en: Arjuna's comprehensive rejection of worldly rewards — victory, kingdom, pleasures — shows his complete disillusionment with the conventional goals of warfare. The rhetorical question about what use these things are when family members fight each other reveals his prioritization of human connection over political power. This moment represents the beginning of Arjuna's transformation from warrior to seeker of truth.

His declaration that he would not kill them even if attacked represents a radical rejection of self-defense as justification for violence.

sanskrit_sloka: ['ఆచార్యాః పితరః పుత్రాస్తథైవ చ పితామహాః ।\nమాతులాః శ్వశురాః పౌత్రాః శ్యాలాః సంబంధినస్తథా ।। 34 ।।', 'ఏతాన్న హంతుమిఛ్చామి ఘ్నఽతోపి మధుసూదన ।\nఅపి త్రైలోక్య రాజ్యస్య హేతోః కిం ను మహీకృతే ।। 35 ।।']
translation_en: Gurus, fathers, sons, uncles, grandsons, uncles, brothers-in-law and other relatives risk their lives and money and come here.  O Madhusudana, even if they attack me I will not kill them. If we kill the sons of Dhritarashtra and gain dominion over the mountains, what satisfaction will we have, and what will I say for the sake of this earth?
explanation_en: Arjuna's statement that 'even if they attack me, I will not kill them' represents a principled stand against violence regardless of provocation or self-defense claims. His observation that killing the sons of Dhritarashtra would bring only guilt and sorrow shows his understanding of karmic consequence and moral responsibility. The mention of teachers and fathers highlights the violation of social hierarchies and sacred relationships that war entails.

sanskrit_sloka: ['నిహత్య ధార్తరాష్ట్రాన్నః కా ప్రీతిః \xa0స్యాజ్జనార్దన ।\nపాపమేవాశ్రయేదస్మాన్ హత్వైతానాతతాయినః ।। 36 ।।', 'తస్మాన్నార్హా వయం హంతుం ధార్తరాష్ట్రాన్ స్వబాంధవాన్ ।\nస్వజనం హి కథం హత్వా సుఖినః స్యామ మాధవ ।। 37 ।।']
translation_en: O Janardhana (protector and patron of all demons), how can we be happy after killing the sons of Dhritarashtra? Even if they are evil aggressors, if we kill them, we will surely be covered with sin. So it is not proper for us to kill Dhritarashtra's sons and friends. O Madhva (Krishna), how can we be happy by killing our own?
explanation_en: Arjuna's observation that while the enemy side may not see the sin in their greed-driven actions, he and his brothers clearly recognize the error of killing family, highlights the responsibility that comes with greater knowledge. His question about why they should not avoid this sinful act when they can clearly see it represents the burden of conscience upon those who know better.

translation_en: They see no fault in greed corrupting their thoughts and destroying their relatives, or in betraying their friends by taking sides. But, O Janardhana, why should not we, who can clearly see the error in killing ourselves, avoid this sinful act?
explanation_en: Arjuna's warning that destroying the family structure destroys all social traditions and moral principles that hold civilization together shows his understanding that social cohesion depends fundamentally on family bonds and obligations. His observation that evil deeds destroy family tradition and create unwanted children reveals the cascading consequences of violence across generations.

translation_en: When the lineage is destroyed, all lineages disappear; The rest of the family members are unrighteous.
explanation_en: Arjuna's description of how the increase of unwanted children degrades both the family line and the very people who destroyed it through their sinful actions shows his belief that moral corruption brings punishment in both this world and beyond. His mention of ancestors being denied proper rites because of lineage destruction reveals the intergenerational impact of violence.

అధర్మాభిభవాత్ కృష్ణ ప్రదుష్యంతి కులస్త్రియః ।
స్త్రీషు దుష్టాసు వార్ష్ణేయ జాయతే వర్ణసంకరః ।। 41 ।।
translation_en: Due to the predominance of vices, O Krishna, caste women become unrighteous, and due to the immoral conduct of women, O Vrishni, unwanted offspring are born.
explanation_en: Arjuna's observation that the destruction of family traditions by evil deeds creates a cycle of spiritual degradation that affects entire communities shows his understanding of how violence undermines the foundations of civilization itself. His reference to unwanted children being born from corrupt unions reveals the biological dimension of moral consequences.

sanskrit_sloka:
సంకరో నరకాయైవ కులఘ్నానాం కులస్య చ ।
పతంతి పితరో హ్యేషాం లుప్తపిండోదకక్రియాః ।। 42 ।।
translation_en: Due to the increase of unwanted children, the caste and also those who destroyed the caste will be in hell. Even those depraved lineage ancestors will fall because of Shraddha tarpanams.
explanation_en: Arjuna's recall of the teachings of wise men that those who destroy family lineages face severe and prolonged punishment in the afterlife shows his acceptance of karmic consequences that extend far beyond a single lifetime. His reference to hearing from scholars establishes that his moral position is grounded in established wisdom and tradition rather than mere personal opinion.

ఉత్సాద్యంతే జాతిధర్మాః కులధర్మాశ్చ శాశ్వతాః ।। 43 ।।
translation_en: Many social and family welfare virtues are destroyed due to their evil deeds which destroy the family tradition and cause unwanted children.
explanation_en: Arjuna's horror at the realization that they are prepared to commit such a grave sin against their own family and tradition shows his shock at having come so close to moral catastrophe through their planning and preparation. His acknowledgment that they were ready to kill relatives for kingdom pleasures reveals the seductive power of ambition over moral judgment.

ఉత్సన్నకులధర్మాణామ్ మనుష్యాణాం జనార్ధన ।
నరకేఽనియతం వాసో భవతీత్యనుశుశ్రుమ ।। 44 ।।
translation_en: O Janardhana (Krishna), I have heard from the scholars that those who destroy castes will remain in hell indefinitely;
explanation_en: Arjuna's conclusion that it would be better to be killed unarmed on the battlefield than to kill his own relatives for worldly gain represents the ultimate rejection of the warrior ethos in favor of moral integrity and compassion. His willingness to die rather than commit injustice shows the depth and sincerity of his conviction about the sanctity of life.

explanation_en: Arjuna's astonishment that they have decided to commit such a terrible sin of killing their own kinsmen shows his shock at having been willing to participate in what he now recognizes as a grievous moral wrong. His statement about being ready to kill relatives for the pleasures of the kingdom exposes the hollowness of material ambition when weighed against human bonds.

explanation_en: Arjuna's continued expression of horror at their willingness to commit such a grave sin for the sake of a kingdom reiterates his position that even if the sons of Dhritarashtra were to slay him while he stood unarmed and unresisting, that would be far preferable to the alternative. His willingness to accept personal destruction rather than cause it demonstrates a complete transformation of values.

sanskrit_sloka:
సంజయ ఉవాచ ।
ఏవముక్త్వార్జునః సంఖ్యే రథోపస్థ ఉపావిశత్ ।
విసృజ్య సశరం చాపం శోకసంవిగ్నమానసః ।। 47 ।।
translation_en: Sanjaya uttered: Thus uttered Arjuna, in a state of dejection, deeply grieved, threw aside his arrows and bow, and collapsed in the chariot.
explanation_en: Arjuna throwing aside his bow and arrows and collapsing in the chariot symbolizes his complete rejection of the warrior's role in this conflict. His collapse shows that this is not a strategic retreat but a genuine spiritual and emotional breakdown. The image of the greatest warrior of his age reduced to a heap of grief demonstrates the power of moral conscience over martial conditioning. This moment of total surrender creates the opening for Krishna's transformative teaching that will form the rest of the Bhagavad Gita.

sanskrit_sloka:
సంజయ ఉవాచ ।
తం తథా కృపయావిష్టమశ్రుపూర్ణాకులేక్షణమ్ ।
విషీదంతమిదం వాక్యమువాచ మధుసూదనః ।। 1 ।।
translation_en: Sanjaya spoke: Seeing Arjuna full of pity, with a sorrowful heart and eyes full of water, Lord Krishna spoke thus.
explanation_en: Sanjaya's observation of Arjuna's tearful, sorrowful heart isn't just reporting — it's establishing the emotional stakes. This isn't a man having a bad day; this is someone whose entire worldview has collapsed. Krishna's decision to speak at this precise moment shows he understands that Arjuna is finally receptive to deeper truth. The chariot positioned between the armies becomes the setting for one of history's most profound spiritual conversations.

sanskrit_sloka:
శ్రీ భగవానువాచ  ।
కుతస్త్వాకశ్మలమిదం విషమే సముపస్థితమ్  ।
అనార్యజుష్టమస్వర్గ్యమ్ అకీర్తికరమర్జున ।। 2 ।।
translation_en: Sri Bhagavan said: Dear Arjuna, at such a critical time, how did this illusion of mind hide itself? This is unbecoming of a respectable person. This does not lead to the best results, but it can lead to scandal.
explanation_en: Krishna's opening question — how has this delusion overtaken you — isn't just concern; it's a challenge. The phrase 'unbecoming of a respectable person' attacks Arjuna's self-image as a noble warrior and thinker. Krishna's observation that this leads 'not to heaven but to disgrace' shows his understanding of how weakness appears to society. But this apparent criticism is actually the beginning of compassion as Krishna prepares to elevate Arjuna's understanding.

sanskrit_sloka:
క్లైబ్యం మా స్మ గమః పార్థ నైతత్త్వయ్యుపపద్యతే  ।
క్షుద్రం హృదయ దౌర్బల్యం త్యక్త్వోత్తిష్ఠ  పరంతప  ।। 3 ।।
translation_en: O Partha, it is not fit for you to surrender to this cowardly self. Abandon this wretched weakness of heart, and go forth to battle, O conqueror of foes.
explanation_en: Krishna's direct command to abandon cowardice and weakness of heart isn't dismissal — it's a challenge to overcome the paralysis of moral confusion. By calling him 'conqueror of foes,' he invokes Arjuna's own experience as evidence that he is capable of more than this collapse. The command to 'go forth to battle' represents not a military order but a challenge to face the situation with courage and clarity.

sanskrit_sloka:
అర్జున ఉవాచ ।
కథం భీష్మమహం సంఖ్యే ద్రోణం చ మధుసూదన ।
ఇషుభి ప్రతియోత్స్యామి పూజార్హవరిసూదన ।। 4 ।।
translation_en: Arjuna said: O Madhusudana, how can I shoot arrows in battle against the venerable Bhishma and Dronacharya? O destroyer of enemies.
explanation_en: Arjuna's response explains the specific moral impossibility of fighting against his revered teachers Bhishma and Dronacharya. The address 'O Madhusudana' appeals to Krishna's role as protector while acknowledging Krishna's own martial history. His question 'how can I shoot arrows' reveals that his objection is not cowardice but deep moral principle rooted in gratitude and respect.

sanskrit_sloka:
గురూనహత్వా హి మహానుభావాన్
శ్రేయో భోక్తుం భైక్ష్యమపీహ లోకే ।
హత్వార్థకామాంస్తు గురూనిహైవ
భుంజీయ భోగాన్ రుధిరప్రదిగ్ధాన్ ।। 5 ।।
translation_en: It is better to live as a beggar than to kill these elders who are my teachers and enjoy these pleasures. If we kill them, our wealth, pleasures, and blood will be tainted.
explanation_en: Arjuna's argument that it would be better to live as a beggar than to enjoy pleasures purchased with the blood of his elders establishes his moral hierarchy where poverty is infinitely preferable to injustice. His observation that their wealth and pleasures would be tainted by the sin of killing teachers shows his understanding of how means determine the quality of ends.

యద్వా జయేమ యది వా నో జయేయుః ।
యానేవ హత్వా న జిజీవిషామః

translation_en: We do not even know which outcome of this war is better for us - to conquer them or to be conquered by them. Even after killing them we don't feel like living. However, they joined the side of Dhritarashtra and stood in front of us on the battlefield.
explanation_en: Arjuna's complete uncertainty about the outcome of the war shows his recognition that both winning and losing could lead to suffering and regret. His observation that killing enemies would not make him want to live reveals the spiritual emptiness of revenge and conquest. This verse captures the paralysis that comes from seeing through the illusions of worldly conflict.

యచ్చ్రేయః  స్యాన్నిశ్చితం బ్రూహి తన్మే
శిష్యస్తేఽహం  శాధి  మాం త్వాం ప్రపన్నమ్  ।। 7 ।।
translation_en: I did not know what my duty was and anxiety and timidity seized me. I am your disciple and your devotee. Teach me what is really good for me.
explanation_en: Arjuna's admission that he has lost clarity about his duty and his appeal to Krishna for guidance represents the essential precondition for receiving genuine wisdom. His declaration 'I am your disciple' establishes the teacher-student relationship that frames the rest of the dialogue. By asking 'what is really good for me,' he shifts the question from tactical military strategy to spiritual well-being.

న హి ప్రపశ్యామి మమాపనుద్యాత్
యఛ్చోకముఛ్చోషణమింద్రియాణామ్ ।
అవాప్య భూమావసపత్నమృద్ధం
రాజ్యం సురాణామపి చాధిపత్యమ్ ।। 8 ।।
translation_en: There is no way to get rid of this grief that dries up my senses. Even if I win an opulent, unrivaled kingdom on this earth and rule like the gods, I cannot remove this sorrow.
explanation_en: Arjuna's declaration that even an unrivaled kingdom ruling like the gods could not dispel his overwhelming grief shows that his distress transcends ordinary disappointment. The phrase 'dries up my senses' reveals the physical and psychological devastation caused by his moral crisis. His recognition that no worldly power can resolve this inner turmoil establishes the need for a completely different kind of solution.

sanskrit_sloka:
సంజయ ఉవాచ ।
ఏవముక్త్వా హృషీకేశం గుడాకేశః పరంతప ।
న యోత్స్య ఇతి గోవిందముక్త్వా తూష్ణీం బభూవ హ ।। 9 ।।
translation_en: Sanjaya spoke: thus Gudakesha, the chastiser of enemies, fell silent, saying to Hrishikesh: "Govinda, I will not fight."
explanation_en: Arjuna falling silent after declaring he will not fight shows the contrast between his warrior identity and current state of confusion. His final declaration 'Govinda, I will not fight' represents the culmination of his moral argument against the war. The silence that follows indicates he has reached the limit of his own understanding and now awaits Krishna's response.

sanskrit_sloka:
తమువాచ హృషికేశః ప్రహసన్నివ భారత ।
సేనయోరుభయోర్మధ్యే విషీదంతమిదం వచః ।। 10 ।।
translation_en: O Dhritarashtra! After that, in the midst of the two armies, Lord Krishna spoke to the grieving Arjuna.
explanation_en: Sanjaya's narration that Krishna begins speaking to the grieving Arjuna between the two assembled armies establishes the setting for the transformative teaching that will follow. The description of Arjuna as 'grieving' establishes his emotional state as the starting point for the teaching. Krishna's decision to speak at this moment shows his understanding that Arjuna is finally ready to listen and learn.

sanskrit_sloka:
శ్రీ భగవానువాచ ।
అశోచ్యానన్వశోచస్త్వం ప్రజ్ఞావాదాంశ్చ భాషసే ।
గతాసూనగతాసూంశ్చ నానుశోచంతి పండితాః ।। 11 ।।
translation_en: The Lord said: You speak words of wisdom but mourn for that which should not be mourned.  The wise mourn neither the dead nor the living.
explanation_en: Krishna's opening observation that Arjuna 'speaks wisely yet mourns for what should not be mourned by the truly learned' establishes the central theme of the soul's immortality. The apparent contradiction between wise speech and foolish grief suggests that Arjuna's understanding is incomplete despite his intelligence. Krishna's opening statement challenges the fundamental assumption that physical death is the ultimate tragedy.

sanskrit_sloka:
న త్వేవాహం జాతు నాసం న త్వం నేమే జనాధిపాః ।
న చైవ న భవిష్యామః సర్వే వయమతః పరమ్ ।। 12 ।।
translation_en: There was no time when I, but you, and all these kings were not; We will not be absent even before.
explanation_en: Krishna's declaration that there was never a time when he, Arjuna, or the assembled kings did not exist challenges the assumption that life begins at birth and ends at death. The inclusive 'we' suggests that all beings share this eternal nature regardless of their current circumstances. By asserting continuous existence, Krishna undermines the foundation of Arjuna's grief about potential death.

sanskrit_sloka:
దేహినోఽస్మిన్ యథా దేహే కౌమారం యౌవనం జరా ।
తథా దేహాంతరప్రాప్తిః ధీరస్తత్ర న ముహ్యతి ।। 13 ।।
translation_en: However, just as the soul in the body passes through childhood, youth and old age respectively, similarly at the time of death, the soul enters another body (body). Wise people do not worry about this.
explanation_en: Krishna's analogy of the soul passing through childhood, youth, and old age — changing bodies at death like changing garments — frames death as a natural transition rather than an ending. The comparison to seasonal change suggests that death is part of a natural cycle. The statement that 'wise people do not worry about this' establishes emotional equanimity as a mark of spiritual understanding.

sanskrit_sloka:
మాత్రాస్పర్శాస్తు కౌంతేయ శీతోష్ణసుఖదుఃఖదాః ।

translation_en: O son of Kunti, due to association with sense-objects, the senses seem to have fleeting, eternal pleasures and sorrows. These are infinities; They come like summer and winter. O descendant of Bharata, learn to bear these things without getting upset.
explanation_en: Krishna's advice to endure the fleeting pleasures and pains that come from contact with sense objects, comparing them to summer and winter, establishes equanimity as a spiritual practice. The analogy to seasons suggests that all experiences are temporary and cyclical. The instruction to 'bear these without being upset' establishes that tolerance can be developed through understanding the transient nature of all sensory experience.

sanskrit_sloka:

translation_en: O Arjuna, the best of men, he who is unaffected by pleasures and sorrows, and is unmoved by both, is worthy of salvation.
explanation_en: Krishna's declaration that the person unaffected by pleasure and pain, and unmoved by both, is worthy of spiritual liberation, establishes emotional balance as the highest achievement of human life. By linking equanimity directly to liberation, Krishna shows that inner peace is the prerequisite for transcendence. The statement that such a person is 'worthy of salvation' suggests that liberation is earned through wisdom and self-mastery.

sanskrit_sloka:
నాసతో విద్యతే భావో నాభావో విద్యతే సతః ।

translation_en: That which is transitory has no permanence and that which is eternal has no end. Philosophers who have studied the nature of these two have observed this fact.
explanation_en: Krishna's distinction between the temporary and the eternal — the transient has no lasting permanence while the eternal has no end — forms the basis of all subsequent metaphysical teaching in the Gita. The reference to 'philosophers who have studied these two realities' establishes that this knowledge comes through careful investigation. This fundamental distinction provides a framework for understanding the nature of reality itself.

sanskrit_sloka:
అవినాశి తు తద్విద్ధి యేన సర్వమిదం తతమ్ ।
వినాశమవ్యయస్యాస్య న కశ్చిత్ కర్తుమర్హతి ।। 17 ।।
translation_en: Know that it is indestructible which pervades the whole body. No one can destroy the impermanent soul.
explanation_en: Krishna's instruction to know that the indestructible soul pervades the entire physical body as its essential foundation directly addresses Arjuna's fear that he will be destroying souls by killing his enemies. The statement that 'no one can destroy the impermanent soul' establishes its absolute invulnerability to any external force. By identifying the soul as all-pervading, Krishna suggests that it transcends the limitations of individual physical forms.

sanskrit_sloka:

అనాశినోఽప్రమేయస్య తస్మాద్యుధ్యస్వ భారత  ।। 18 ।।
translation_en: Only this physical body is perishable; But the Jivatma is imperishable, immeasurable and Sanatana (Eternal). Therefore, O descendant of Bharata, fight.
explanation_en: Krishna's declaration that only the physical body is perishable while the soul is eternal and absolutely indestructible, followed by the instruction 'therefore fight,' establishes that recognizing the soul's immortality should motivate action rather than paralysis. The command to fight is not a dismissal of moral concerns but a call to act from a higher and more complete understanding of reality.

translation_en: He who thinks that the soul kills others and he who thinks that the soul is killed by others are both ignorant. Indeed the soul does not kill anyone, nor is it killed by anyone.
explanation_en: Krishna's observation that both the person who thinks the soul kills another and the person who thinks the soul is killed by another are fundamentally ignorant challenges the common assumption that violence affects the soul's eternal existence. By declaring that 'the soul neither kills nor is killed,' Krishna transcends the conventional categories of killer and killed entirely.

translation_en: O Partha, who knows that the soul is indestructible, eternal, without birth and death, how can he kill (anyone)? How can he be the cause of death?
explanation_en: Krishna's rhetorical question about how one who truly knows the soul to be indestructible can possibly cause real death suggests that genuine knowledge of the soul's nature eliminates the fear of killing. By linking understanding directly to action, Krishna implies that correct perception naturally and inevitably leads to correct behavior.

translation_en: Just as a human being discards his worn-out old clothes and puts on new clothes, so the soul at the time of death leaves the old body and assumes a new body.
explanation_en: Krishna's analogy of changing clothes to explain how the soul leaves one body and enters another at death makes the abstract concept of reincarnation concrete and immediately accessible. By using this everyday image, Krishna demystifies death and reduces its terror. The implication is that just as clothes do not define the essential person, the physical body does not define the eternal soul.

sanskrit_sloka:
యదృచ్ఛయా చోపపన్నం స్వర్గద్వారమపావృతమ్ ।
సుఖినః క్షత్రియాః పార్థ లభంతే యుద్ధమీదృశమ్ ।। 32 ।।
translation_en: O Partha, the Kshatriyas are fortunate, given the opportunity to preserve the Dharma without seeking it. It is an open door to heaven for them.
explanation_en: Krishna's observation that 'for a Kshatriya there is no greater good than a righteous battle' establishes the warrior's duty as a sacred trust. The statement that 'such a war comes of itself like an open door' suggests that opportunities for righteous action present themselves naturally to those positioned to take them. This verse establishes the warrior's obligation as a privilege rather than a burden.
word_by_word_meaning_en: yadrcchaya — without wanting; Cha — and; sub-income — received; svarga — heavenly worlds; द्वराम — the door; apavartam — open; sukhinah — happiness; kshatriyah — the kshatriya heroes; Partha — Arjuna, son of Pritha; labhante — is obtained; war — war; This is like this.

sanskrit_sloka:
అథ చేత్త్వమిమం ధర్మ్యం సంగ్రామం న కరిష్యసి ।
తతః స్వధర్మం కీర్తిం చ హిత్వా పాపమవాప్స్యసి ।। 33 ।।
translation_en: But if you leave your self-righteousness and glory and refuse to fight this righteous war, you will surely become a sinner.
explanation_en: Krishna's statement that 'if you do not fight this righteous battle, you will fail in your duty and lose your reputation' establishes the social consequences of abandoning one's position. The observation that 'your reputation will be destroyed' connects individual action to public perception. This verse establishes that duty is not just personal but has social dimensions.
word_by_word_meaning_en: atha chet — but if; tvam — you; imam — this; Dharmya Sangramam — Dharma War; na karishyasi — don't do it; tatah — after that; sva-dharma — self-righteousness (duty prescribed by the Vedas); kirtim — renown; Cha — and; hitwa — leave; sin — sin; avapsyasi — will get.

sanskrit_sloka:
అకీర్తిం చాపి భూతాని
కథయిష్యంతి తేఽవ్యయామ్
సంభావితస్య చాకీర్తిః
మరణాదతిరిచ్యతే ।। 34 ।।
translation_en: People call you a coward and a deserter. To an honorable man dishonor is worse than death.
explanation_en: Krishna's observation that 'people will talk about your disgrace forever' establishes the lasting impact of abandoning one's duty. The statement that 'for a respected person, disgrace is worse than death' establishes a moral hierarchy where honor is valued above physical survival. This verse establishes that social reputation has spiritual significance.
word_by_word_meaning_en: akirtim — infamy; Cha — and; api — also; bhutani — the people; kathaishyanti — called; te — of you; avyam — eternally abiding; sambhavatasya — to the respectable; Cha — and; akirtih — infamy; marinat — than death; atirichyate — excessive.

sanskrit_sloka:
భయాద్రణాదుపరతం మంస్యంతే త్వాం మహారథాః ।
యేషాం చ త్వం బహుమతో భూత్వా యాస్యసి లాఘవమ్ ।। 35 ।।
translation_en: Great are you in the eyes of the great charioteers, who, fearing you, flee from the battlefield. You will lose their respect for you.
explanation_en: Krishna's observation that 'great warriors will think you fled from battle out of fear' shows how your actions will be interpreted by others. The statement that 'those who have greatly respected you will think you are worthless' establishes the loss of social standing as a consequence of inaction. This verse establishes that others' perceptions matter in the moral calculus.
word_by_word_meaning_en: bhayat — with fear; ranat — from the land of war; uparatam — running away; mansyante — thinks; tvam — you; Mahārāthāḥ — having strength equal to ten thousand ordinary warriors; yesham — to whom; Cha — and; tvam — you; bahumatah — the great respected one; bhutva — have become; yasyasi — you lose; Laghavam — a sneer.

sanskrit_sloka:
అవాచ్యవాదాంశ్చ బహూన్ వదిష్యన్తి తవాహితాః ।
నిందంతస్తవ సామర్థ్యమ్ తతో దుఃఖతరం ను కిమ్ ।। 36 ।।
translation_en: Your enemies will slander you and insult you with cruel words, thereby diminishing your greatness. Ugh, is there anything more painful than this?
explanation_en: Krishna's description of the 'unkind words' that will be spoken by those who have greatly respected you establishes the verbal abuse that will follow perceived cowardice. The observation that 'your enemies will describe you in many unkind words' shows the social punishment for abandoning your position. This verse establishes that verbal abuse is a real consequence of inaction.
word_by_word_meaning_en: avacya-vadan — with unspoken words (harsh words); Cha — and; bahoon — a lot; vadisyanti — is called; tava — of you; ahitah — enemies; nindantah — accuse; tava — of you; குத்திய்முத்து — the ability; tatah — more than that; duhkha-taram — more suffering; nu — truly; Kim — What.

sanskrit_sloka:
హతో వా ప్రాప్స్యసి స్వర్గం జిత్వా వా భోక్షసే మహీమ్ ।
తస్మాదుత్తిష్ఠ కౌంతేయ యుద్ధాయ కృతనిశ్చయః ।। 37 ।।
translation_en: If you fight, you will die a heroic death on the battlefield and go to heaven, or you will enjoy this kingdom as a victor. Therefore, be determined, O son of Kunti, and prepare for battle.
explanation_en: Krishna's observation that 'killing you will bring you a heavenly abode, while victory will bring you enjoyment of the earth' establishes the win-win nature of fighting from a duty perspective. The statement that 'therefore, arise with determination and fight' presents the choice as obvious. This verse establishes that fighting is the only rational choice for a warrior.
word_by_word_meaning_en: hatah — when killed; wa — or; propsyasi — you get; svargam — heaven; jitva — if won; wa — or; bhokshyase — experience; mahim — this earthly kingdom; tasmat — so; uttishtha — lemmu; Kaunteya — Arjuna, son of Kunti; yudhaya — for war; krita-nischaya — with firm determination.

sanskrit_sloka:
సుఖదుఃఖే సమే కృత్వా లాభాలాభౌ జయాజయౌ ।
తతో యుద్ధాయ యుజ్యస్వ నైవం పాపమవాప్స్యసి ।। 38 ।।
translation_en: Take the joys and sorrows, profit and loss equally - fight as duty. By performing your duties in this way you will never feel guilty.
explanation_en: Krishna's instruction to 'fight, treating pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike' establishes the principle of equanimity in action. The statement that 'by doing this you will not incur sin' establishes that detachment from results is what makes action righteous. This verse establishes karma yoga as the path of action without attachment.
word_by_word_meaning_en: sukha — pleasures; dukhe — sorrows; same krtva — considered equal; labha-alabhau — profit and loss; Jaya-ajayau — victory and defeat; tatah — after a; yudhaya — for war; Yujyasva — Siddhavau Aumu; na — not; evam — thus; sin — sin; avapsyasi — get.

sanskrit_sloka:
ఏషా తేఽభిహితా సాంఖ్యే
బుద్ధిర్యోగే త్విమాం శృణు ।
బుధ్ధ్యా యుక్తో యయా పార్థ
కర్మబంధం ప్రహాస్యసి ।। 39 ।।
translation_en: So far I have explained to you Sankhya Yoga, i.e., the analytical knowledge of Atma Tattva. Now listen, O Partha, I will explain Buddhi Yoga. When you act with this awareness you will be freed from karmic bonds.
explanation_en: Krishna's observation that 'this wisdom has been revealed to you as Sankhya' establishes that what he's teaching is part of an established philosophical tradition. The statement that 'now listen to the wisdom of yoga' suggests that there is a complementary approach. This verse establishes that both knowledge and action are valid paths.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Aesha — so far; te — to you; abhiṭha — that which is known; sankhye — by analytical knowledge; buddhih -yoge — by buddhi yoga; tu — truly; Imam — this; srinu — hear; buddhya — by understanding; yuktah — together; yaya — because of what; Partha — Arjuna, son of Fritha; karmabandham — karmic bond; prahasyasi — from which thou art freed.

sanskrit_sloka:
నేహాభిక్రమనాశోఽస్తి ప్రత్యవాయో న విద్యతే ।
స్వల్పమప్యస్య ధర్మస్య త్రాయతే మహతో భయాత్ ।। 40 ।।
translation_en: When working with this perspective, there is no harm but opposite results. Even a little practice can save us from big dangers.
explanation_en: Krishna's declaration that 'in this path there is no loss of effort, no fear of backsliding' establishes the security of the spiritual path. The observation that 'even a little of this dharma protects one from great fear' establishes that partial practice is still valuable. This verse establishes that the spiritual path is safe and accessible.
word_by_word_meaning_en: na — not; eha — in which; abhikrama — efforts; nasah — loss; asti — will be; pratyavayah — negative results; na — not; vidyate — will be; su-alpam — a little; api — also; asya — of this; dharmasya — of dharma; trayate — protects; mahatah — great; Bhayat — danger.

sanskrit_sloka:
వ్యవసాయాత్మికా బుద్దిరేకేహ కురునందన ।
బహుశాఖా హ్యనంతాశ్చ బుద్ధయోఽవ్యవసాయినామ్ ।। 41 ।।
translation_en: O descendant of Kuru, those on this path are steadfast in their minds, their goal is one. But, the mind of those who are not fixed will be in the way of surroundings.
explanation_en: Krishna's observation that 'the resolute determination to realize the Self is single-pointed' establishes the importance of focused intention. The statement that 'the irresolute have many thoughts' shows the difference between those who are committed and those who are not. This verse establishes that determination is key to spiritual progress.
word_by_word_meaning_en: agrarian-atmika — sturdy; buddhih — the mind; eka — one; eha — in this path; kuru-nandana — son of Kuru; bahu-sakhah — many-branched; hi — truly; anantah — endless; Cha — and; buddhayaḥ — the mind; avyavasainam — without strong will.

sanskrit_sloka: ['యామిమాం పుష్పితాం వాచం ప్రవదంత్యవిపశ్చితః ।\nవేదవాదరతాః పార్థ నాన్యదస్తీతి వాదినః ।। 42 ।।', 'కామాత్మానః స్వర్గపరా జన్మకర్మఫలప్రదామ్ ।\nక్రియావిశేషబహులాం భోగైశ్వర్యగతిం ప్రతి ।। 43 ।।']
translation_en: Those of limited understanding are attracted by the seductive words of the Vedas, which refer to pretentious rituals for the attainment of the heavenly world, and think that there is nothing higher in it. They glorify those parts of the Vedas that bring them sensual pleasures and perform extravagant rituals for higher birth, wealth, sensual pleasures, access to the heavenly world, etc.
explanation_en: Krishna's dismissal of 'flowery speech' from the Vedas that promises rewards shows his understanding that scripture can be misinterpreted. The observation that 'those with material desires seek heaven' establishes the limitation of goal-oriented spirituality. This verse establishes that true spirituality is not about gaining rewards.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Am-imam — all these; pushpitam — attractive; vacham — words; pravadanti — is called; avipascitah — of limited understanding; veda-vada-ratah — interested in the fruition of the Veda; Partha — Arjuna, son of Pritha; na anyat asti — there is nothing else; iti — in this way; vadinah — argue; kama-atmanah — longing for physical pleasures; svarga-parah — the goal of attaining the heavenly worlds; janma-karma-phala — best birth, good results; pradam — giving; kriya-visesha — pretentious karmic stems; bahulam — many; bhoga — indulgences; Aishwarya — riches; gatim — progress; on each — side.

sanskrit_sloka: ['యామిమాం పుష్పితాం వాచం ప్రవదంత్యవిపశ్చితః ।\nవేదవాదరతాః పార్థ నాన్యదస్తీతి వాదినః ।। 42 ।।', 'కామాత్మానః స్వర్గపరా జన్మకర్మఫలప్రదామ్ ।\nక్రియావిశేషబహులాం భోగైశ్వర్యగతిం ప్రతి ।। 43 ।।']
translation_en: Those of limited understanding are attracted by the seductive words of the Vedas, which refer to pretentious rituals for the attainment of the heavenly world, and think that there is nothing higher in it. They glorify those parts of the Vedas that bring them sensual pleasures and perform extravagant rituals for higher birth, wealth, sensual pleasures, access to the heavenly world, etc.
explanation_en: Krishna's observation that 'the Vedas are full of elaborate rituals for obtaining various powers and pleasures' acknowledges the traditional religious practice of his time. The statement that 'rebirth is the result' establishes that these practices keep one bound to the cycle. This verse establishes that ritual alone is insufficient for liberation.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Am-imam — all these; pushpitam — attractive; vacham — words; pravadanti — is called; avipascitah — of limited understanding; veda-vada-ratah — interested in the fruition of the Veda; Partha — Arjuna, son of Pritha; na anyat asti — there is nothing else; iti — in this way; vadinah — argue; kama-atmanah — longing for physical pleasures; svarga-parah — the goal of attaining the heavenly worlds; janma-karma-phala — best birth, good results; pradam — giving; kriya-visesha — pretentious karmic stems; bahulam — many; bhoga — indulgences; Aishwarya — riches; gatim — progress; on each — side.

sanskrit_sloka:
భోగైశ్వర్యప్రసక్తానాం తయాపహృతచేతసామ్ ।
వ్యవసాయాత్మికా బుద్ధిః సమాధౌ న విధీయతే ।। 44 ।।
translation_en: With much attachment to worldly pleasures and pleasures, their minds become delusional and they cannot have the firm will required for success in the path of Bhagavadprapti.
explanation_en: Krishna's warning that 'those who are attached to pleasures and powers are attracted by such things and cannot have the determination for Self-realization' establishes the obstacle that desire creates. The observation that 'the mind is not steady' shows how attachment disturbs concentration. This verse establishes that desire is the enemy of spiritual progress.
word_by_word_meaning_en: bhoga — indulgences; aishvarya — towards luxuries; prasaktanam — for those who are very passionate; taya — because of that; apahruta-chetasam — with a bewildered mind; agraha-atmika — determined; buddhih — the mind; samadhau — accomplishment; na — not; Vidhiate — does not stand.

sanskrit_sloka:
త్రైగుణ్యవిషయా వేదా నిస్త్రైగుణ్యో భవార్జున ।
నిర్ద్వంద్వో నిత్యసత్వస్థో నిర్యోగక్షేమ ఆత్మవాన్ ।। 45 ।।
translation_en: Arjuna, the Vedas explain the three-fold subjectivity of physical nature. Be thou in a state of pure spiritual knowledge beyond these trigunas. Detach from dualities, be eternally established in the Supreme Truth, and remain steadfast in the sense of self, regardless of material gains and security.
explanation_en: Krishna's instruction to 'free yourself from the three gunas' establishes the goal of transcending material nature. The observation that 'the Vedas deal with the gunas' acknowledges the utility of scripture while recognizing its limitations. The instruction to 'be established in the Self without worrying about obtaining and preserving' establishes non-attachment as the practical application.
word_by_word_meaning_en: trigunya — three-fold of physical nature; vishaya — things; veda — the Vedas; nistrai gunyo — beyond the trigunas; bhava — be; Arjuna — Arjuna; nirdvandvah — beyond dualities (like harshasoka); nitya-sattva-sthah — eternally established in truth; niryoga-kshema — unconcerned about the benefits of yoga; atma-van — state of the soul.

sanskrit_sloka:
యావానర్థ ఉదపానే సర్వతః సంప్లుతోదకే ।
తావాన్సర్వేషు వేదేషు బ్రాహ్మణస్య విజానతః ।। 46 ।।
translation_en: All the advantages of a small water well can naturally be obtained with a large pool of water. In this way he who knows the supreme truth and attains Bhagavat attains the goal of all the Vedas.
explanation_en: Krishna's analogy that 'a well is of no use to one whose thirst is already quenched' illustrates the limitation of scriptural knowledge when direct realization has been achieved. The observation that 'such a person has already transcended the Vedas' establishes that direct experience supersedes textual study. This verse establishes that knowledge becomes irrelevant once its purpose has been served.
word_by_word_meaning_en: yavan — which; artha — necessary; uda-pane — the water well; sarvatah — in all ways; sampluta -udake — a large lake; tawan — that much; sarveshu — in all manner; vedeshu — the Vedas; brahmanasya — the knower of the supreme truth (brahma jnani); vijanatah — of absolute knowledge.

sanskrit_sloka:
కర్మణ్యేవాధికారస్తే మా ఫలేషు కదాచన ।
మా కర్మఫలహేతుర్భూః  మా తే సంగోఽస్త్వకర్మణి ।। 47 ।।
translation_en: You have the authority to perform the ritual duty prescribed by Shastra, but you have no right over the fruits of that karma.  Never think that you are the reason for the fruits of karma and do not be interested in doing the karmas that should be done.
explanation_en: Krishna's famous declaration 'you have the right to work alone, never to its fruits' establishes the fundamental principle of karma yoga. The instruction 'do not let the fruits of action be your motive' removes the ego from the equation. The warning 'do not be attached to inaction' prevents the misinterpretation that duty should be abandoned.
word_by_word_meaning_en: karmani — before prescribed (Vedavihita) karma; eva — only; adhikarah — right; te — to you; ma — no; faleshu — in its fruits; kadachana — even always; Ma — not; karma phala — fruits of karma; hetuh — cause; bhuh — yes; ma — should not; te — of you; sangah — interest (mamakara); astu — being; Akarmani — performing karma.

sanskrit_sloka:
యోగస్థః  కురు కర్మాణి సంగం త్యక్త్వా ధనంజయ ।
సిద్ధ్య సిద్ధ్యోః  సమో భూత్వా సమత్వం యోగ ఉచ్యతే ।। 48 ।।
translation_en: Be steadfast in the performance of your duty, O Arjuna. Such equanimity is called yoga.
explanation_en: Krishna's instruction to 'establish in yoga and perform action' establishes the integration of meditation and daily life. The observation that 'yoga is evenness of mind' defines the state to be achieved. The statement that 'remaining even-minded in success and failure' establishes equanimity as the practical manifestation of yoga.
word_by_word_meaning_en: yoga-sthah — being fixed in yoga; kuru — do; karmani — karmas (duties) sangam — mamakaram (interest); tyaktva — abandoning (giving up); Dhananjaya — Arjuna; siddhi-asiddyoh — in winning and losing; samah — being even; bhutva — having; samatva — equanimity; yogah — yoga; Uchyate — will be told.

sanskrit_sloka:
దూరేణ హ్యవరం కర్మ బుద్ధియోగాద్ధనంజయ ।
బుద్ధౌ శరణమన్విచ్ఛ కృపణాః ఫలహేతవః  ।। 49 ।।
translation_en: Take refuge in divine spiritual knowledge. O Arjuna, give up fruitive actions; They are of a lower order than those which keep the mind fixed in spiritual divine knowledge. Those who want to enjoy the fruits of their karma are greedy/hungry.
explanation_en: Krishna's observation that 'far lower than yoga is action' establishes the hierarchy of spiritual practice. The instruction 'seek refuge in the wisdom of the Self' establishes knowledge as superior to action alone. The observation that 'pitiable are those who work for the fruits of action' shows the limitation of goal-oriented behavior.
word_by_word_meaning_en: doorena — (relinquish) from a distance; hi — truly; avaram — lower level; karma — actions done with a desire for fruition; Buddhi-Yogat — divine spiritual knowledge by keeping the mind fixed; Dhananjaya — Arjuna; buddhau — spiritual knowledge, insight;  शारानाम — asyrah(asylum); anvicchha — seek; kripanah — greedy/greedy; Phalahetavah — those who expect the fruits of karma.

sanskrit_sloka:
బుద్ధియుక్తో జహాతీహ ఉభే సుకృతదుష్కృతే ।
తస్మాద్యోగాయ యుజ్యస్వ యోగః కర్మసు కౌశలమ్ ।। 50 ।।
translation_en: One who wisely practices this Karma Shastra will renounce both the virtues and sins in this very birth. So practice yoga, which means working with skill (with right attitude).
explanation_en: Krishna's declaration that 'one who has wisdom in this world casts off both good and evil karma' establishes the transcendent nature of spiritual knowledge. The instruction 'therefore, devote yourself to yoga' establishes yoga as the practical path. This verse establishes that wisdom frees one from the karmic cycle.
word_by_word_meaning_en: buddhi-yuktah — having knowledge; jahati — give up; eha — in that birth; ubhe — both; sukrita-dushkrite — good and bad deeds; tasmat — so; yogaya — for yoga; yujyasva — attempt; Yogah — Yoga means; Karmasu Kaushalam — The art of working with skill.

sanskrit_sloka:
కర్మజం బుద్ధియుక్తా హి ఫలం త్వక్త్వా మనీషిణః ।
జన్మబంధవినిర్ముక్తాః పదం గచ్ఛంత్యనామయమ్ ।। 51 ।।
translation_en: The wise, possessing equanimity, have renounced mamkara-interests in the fruits of karma that bind them in the cycle of birth and death. By working with such a feeling, one attains a state of sorrowlessness.
explanation_en: The wise, Krishna says, let go of the personal stake that would otherwise chain them to the endless cycle of birth and death — and the reward isn't some future paradise but a state of sorrowlessness available now. It's a subtle shift in what's being sold: not escape to somewhere else, but relief right where you already are.

sanskrit_sloka:
యదా తే మోహకలిలం బుద్ధిర్వ్యతితరిష్యతి ।
తదా గంతాసి నిర్వేదం శ్రోతవ్యస్య శ్రుతస్య చ ।। 52 ।।
translation_en: Only when your mind is freed from the quicksand of passion, do you feel disillusioned with what you have heard so far and what you are going to hear. (In the case of pleasures of this world).
explanation_en: Krishna's image of the mind crossing beyond the 'quicksand of delusion' captures something about how attachment actually feels from inside it — not like a clear choice but like sinking ground, where every attempt to secure yourself pulls you deeper. Once past it, even things you were eager to hear about lose their grip.

sanskrit_sloka:
శృతివిప్రతి పన్నా తే యదా స్థాస్యతి నిశ్చలా ।
సమాధావచలా బుద్ధిస్తదా యోగామవాప్స్యసి ।। 53 ।।
translation_en: When your mind is fixed on God instead of being attracted to the Vedic sections that tell the stems of Kamya Karma, then you will attain the state of complete yoga.
explanation_en: The contrast here is between a mind scattered by the promises of ritual texts that trade in worldly reward, and a mind settled directly on the divine. Krishna isn't dismissing scripture wholesale — he's pointing out that even sacred texts can become another form of distraction if they're approached for what they can get you rather than where they can take you.

sanskrit_sloka:
అర్జున ఉవాచ ।
స్థితప్రజ్ఞస్య కా భాషా సమాధిస్థస్య కేశవ ।
స్థితధీః కిం ప్రభాషేత కిమాసీత వ్రజేత కిమ్ ।। 54 ।।
translation_en: Arjuna said: O Kesava, what is the disposition of one who is steady (sthitaprajna) of Bhagavat dhyasa nande?  How does an enlightened person speak? How does he sit? How does he walk?
explanation_en: Arjuna's question shifts registers entirely — he stops arguing and starts genuinely curious, wanting to know what a person of steady wisdom actually looks like in practice: how they talk, sit, walk. It's a wonderfully concrete question after pages of abstraction, and it signals he's finally ready to hear something he can actually use.

sanskrit_sloka:
శ్రీ భగవానువాచ ।
ప్రజహాతి యదా కామాన్ సర్వాన్ పార్థ మనోగతాన్ ।
ఆత్మన్యేవాత్మనా తుష్టః స్థితప్రజ్ఞస్తదోచ్యతే ।। 55 ।।
translation_en: Lord Palikenu said: O Partha, when one is satisfied in the knowledge of the Self, abandoning all selfish interests and sensual desires that torment the mind, that person is called Stitha Prajna.
explanation_en: Krishna's answer roots steadiness not in circumstance but in satisfaction — someone who has found completeness in the Self no longer needs anything external to feel whole. The term he introduces, sthita prajna, becomes a kind of technical marker for this state, one he'll spend the rest of the chapter unpacking.

sanskrit_sloka:
దుఃఖేష్వనుద్విగ్నమనాః సుఖేషు విగతస్పృహః ।

translation_en: He who is not disturbed even in the midst of sorrows, who is born for pleasures; One who has given up anger, fear and anger is called a wise sage.
explanation_en: Being undisturbed by sorrow and unmoved even by things designed to give pleasure isn't presented as indifference to life — it's a description of someone who has released anger and fear enough that neither extreme experience destabilizes them. Stability here isn't the absence of feeling; it's the absence of being ruled by it.

sanskrit_sloka:
యః సర్వత్రానభిస్నేహః తత్తత్ ప్రాప్య శుభాశుభమ్ ।

translation_en: He who is disinterested in all situations, does not rejoice in good fortune and is not depressed by hardships, is a sage of perfect knowledge.
explanation_en: Neither elated by fortune nor crushed by hardship — Krishna repeats this theme with slight variation because it's central, not because he's running out of ideas. Each restatement adds a different angle: here the emphasis lands on disinterest across all situations, a kind of even keel that holds regardless of what comes.

sanskrit_sloka:
యదా సంహరతే చాయం కూర్మోంఽగానీవ సర్వశః ।
ఇంద్రియాణీంద్రియార్థేభ్యః తస్య ప్రజ్ఞా ప్రతిష్ఠితా ।। 58 ।।
translation_en: He who can withdraw the senses from their objects, as a tortoise withdraws its limbs into its shell, is fixed in divine spiritual knowledge.
explanation_en: The tortoise pulling its limbs inward gives Arjuna something visual and instinctive to hold onto — an image of protective withdrawal that's neither violent nor passive. Sense-control, in this picture, isn't fighting the senses; it's simply choosing when to extend and when to draw back, the way a tortoise does without struggle.

sanskrit_sloka:
విషయా వినివర్తంతే నిరాహారస్య దేహినః ।
రసవర్జం రసోఽప్యస్య పరం దృష్ట్వా నివర్తతే ।। 59 ।।
translation_en: Even if the Sadhaka controls the senses from the objects of pleasure, the taste remains for the objects of the senses. But, when you understand the philosophy of Bhagwat, that taste also ends.
explanation_en: Krishna makes an important distinction that a lot of self-discipline misses: restraining the senses from objects doesn't automatically kill the taste for those objects. The craving can survive the abstinence. Only a genuine shift in understanding — actually tasting something higher — dissolves the appetite itself, rather than just denying it temporarily.

sanskrit_sloka:
యతతో హ్యపి కౌంతేయ పురుషస్య విపశ్చితః ।
ఇంద్రియాణి ప్రమాథీని హరంతి ప్రసభం మనః ।। 60 ।।
translation_en: The senses are so forceful and turbulent that they can forcibly seize the mind of even a wise and self-controlled sadhaka, O son of Kunti.
explanation_en: This verse functions almost as a caution against overconfidence: even a wise, disciplined practitioner can have their mind forcibly seized by the sheer momentum of the senses. Krishna isn't undermining the practice he's just described; he's warning that mastery isn't a permanent, unassailable state.
