sanskrit_sloka:
సత్త్వం రజస్తమ ఇతి గుణాః ప్రకృతిసంభవాః ।
నిబధ్నంతి మహాబాహో దేహే దేహినమవ్యయమ్ ।। 5 ।।
translation_en: O great-armed Arjuna, the physical nature of energy consists of the three gunas – the sattva guna, the rajo guna, and the tamo guna. It is these qualities that bind the imperishable eternal soul to the perishable body.
explanation_en: Naming the three gunas — sattva, rajas, tamas — as what binds the imperishable soul to the perishable body identifies the actual mechanism of entanglement. It isn't the body alone that traps the soul; it's these three qualities operating through the body that create the bondage.
word_by_word_meaning_en: sattva — quality of sattva; rajah — quality of Rajo; tamah — tamo quality; iti — in this way; gunah — qualities; prakriti — physical nature; sambhavah — having;  nibadhnanti — binds; mahabaho — the one with the great arms; dehe — in the body; dehinam — soul; avyam — orthodox.

sanskrit_sloka:
తత్ర సత్వం నిర్మలత్వాత్ ప్రకాశకమనామయమ్ ।
సుఖ-సంగేన బధ్నాతి జ్ఞానసంగేన చానఘ ।। 6 ।।
translation_en: Among these the sattva guna is holier than the rest, it is luminous and most salutary.  O sinless one, interest in knowledge and pleasure ensnares the soul.
explanation_en: Calling sattva the purest and most luminous of the three, while noting it still binds through attachment to knowledge and happiness, is a genuinely surprising move — even the 'best' guna is named as a form of bondage, just a more refined and pleasant one than the alternatives.
word_by_word_meaning_en: tatra — of which; sattva — quality of sattva; nirmalatvat — because the purest; prasakam — bright; anamayam — wholesome and wholesome; sukha — pleasure; sangena — mamakarasakti; badhnati — binds; jnana — knowledge; sangena — mamakarasakti; Cha — and; Anagha — Arjuna, the sinless one.

sanskrit_sloka:
రజో రాగాత్మకం విద్ధి తృష్ణాసంగసముద్భవమ్ ।
తన్నిబధ్నాతి కౌంతేయ కర్మసంగేన దేహినమ్ ।। 7 ।।
translation_en: O Arjuna, Rajo Guna is full of sensuality. It is born of worldly desires and affections and binds the soul with interest in lustful deeds.
explanation_en: Describing rajas as rooted in craving and attachment, binding the soul through action driven by desire, gives this guna a very recognizable shape — the restless, achievement-oriented energy that most people would associate with an active, ambitious life.
word_by_word_meaning_en: rajah — quality of Rajo; raga-atmakam — the lustful nature; viddhi — know; trishna — desires; sanga — confluence;  samudbhavam — originated;   tat — that; nibadhnati — binds; Kaunteya — Arjuna, son of Kunti; karma-sangena — because of interest in lustful karmas;  Dehinam — Jivatma.

sanskrit_sloka:
తమస్త్వజ్ఞానజం విద్ధి మోహనం సర్వదేహినామ్  ।
ప్రమాదాలస్యనిద్రాభిః  తన్నిబధ్నాతి భారత  ।। 8 ।।
translation_en: O Arjuna, the tamo guna, born of ignorance, is the cause of the delusion of living souls.  It makes all living beings deluded by indifference, laziness and sleep.
explanation_en: Tamas, born of ignorance, is described as deluding through laziness, sleep, and negligence — the quality most people would readily call 'bad,' though Krishna's earlier point about sattva still binding through pleasure suggests none of the three gunas are simply good or evil in isolation.
word_by_word_meaning_en: tamah — tamo quality; tu — but; ajnana-jam — born of ignorance; viddhi — know; mohanam — illusion; sarva-dehinam — to all living beings; शार्ष्ट — carelessness; lasya — laziness; nidrabhih — and sleep; tat — that; nibadhnati — binds; Bharata — Arjuna, descendant of Bharata.

sanskrit_sloka:
సత్త్వం సుఖే సంజయతి రజః కర్మణి భారత ।
జ్ఞానమావృత్య తు తమః ప్రమాదే సంజయత్యుత ।। 9 ।।
translation_en: Sattva binds one to material pleasures; Rajo guna makes the soul interested in karma; And tamo guna covers knowledge and binds one to delusion.
explanation_en: Summarizing the three functions in a single verse — sattva binding through happiness, rajas through action, tamas covering knowledge — gives Arjuna a compact reference point before the chapter moves into more detail about how these forces actually interact and compete.

sanskrit_sloka:
రజస్తమశ్చాభిభూయ సత్త్వం భవతి భారత ।
రజః సత్వం తమశ్చైవ తమః సత్త్వం రజస్తథా ।। 10 ।।
translation_en: Sometimes Sattva has the upper hand over Rajotamas. Sometimes Rajo Guna dominates Sattva and Tamogunas; And some times Tamoguna overcomes Sattvarajo Gunas.
explanation_en: The observation that these gunas constantly shift dominance, with each one temporarily overpowering the others, describes inner life as inherently unstable and fluctuating rather than fixed — no one is simply 'a sattvic person' or 'a rajasic person' permanently; the balance is always in motion.

sanskrit_sloka:
['సర్వద్వారేషు దేహేఽస్మిన్ ప్రకాశ ఉపజాయతే ।
జ్ఞానం యదా తదా విద్యాత్ వివృద్ధం సత్త్వమిత్యుత ।। 11 ।।', 'లోభః ప్రవృత్తిరారంభః కర్మణామశమః స్పృహా ।
రజస్యేతాని జాయంతే వివృద్ధే భరతర్షభ ।। 12 ।।', 'అప్రకాశోఽప్రవృత్తిశ్చ ప్రమాదో మోహ ఏవ చ ।
తమస్యేతాని జాయంతే వివృద్ధే కురునందన ।। 13 ।।']
translation_en: When all the portals of the body are illumined by knowledge, know that it is the manifestation of sattva guna. When Rajo guna prevails, O Arjuna, lobha (greed), industry for worldly gain, depression, and yava increase. O Arjuna – Ignorance, inertia, indifference, and lust – these are the main characteristics of Tamo Guna.
explanation_en: Illumination throughout the body's faculties marks sattva's ascendance — a fairly abstract description, but one that gives a felt sense of clarity and light as the signature of this quality taking the lead over the other two.

O Arjuna – Ignorance, inertia, indifference, and lust – these are the main characteristics of Tamo Guna.
explanation_en: Greed, restless activity, and intense craving for results mark rajas gaining ground, according to this description — a cluster of qualities that would feel, from the inside, like ambition and drive, but described here as symptoms of imbalance rather than simply admirable qualities.

O Arjuna – Ignorance, inertia, indifference, and lust – these are the main characteristics of Tamo Guna.

sanskrit_sloka: ['యదా సత్త్వే పవృద్ధే తు ప్రలయం యాతి దేహభృత్ ।\nతదోత్తమవిదాం లోకాన్ అమలాన్ ప్రతిపద్యతే ।। 14 ।।', 'రజసి ప్రలయం గత్వా కర్మసంగిషు జాయతే ।\nతథా ప్రలీనస్తమసి మూఢయోనిషు జాయతే ।। 15 ।।']
translation_en: Those who are sattva-guna dominant and die reach the holy worlds (without rajas and tamas) where the wise are. Rajo Guna predominates and those who die are born in those who are inspired by deeds; Those who die under the influence of tamo guna are born in animal life.
explanation_en: The claim that dying while sattva predominates leads to rebirth among the wise, while dying under rajas or tamas leads to correspondingly lower outcomes, ties this entire framework to consequences that extend beyond a single lifetime — which guna is active at death carries real weight.

explanation_en: Repeating this same claim about death and rebirth reinforces its importance within the chapter's logic — the state one is in at the final moment isn't treated as incidental but as something shaped by the cumulative pattern of which guna a person has spent their life cultivating.

sanskrit_sloka:
కర్మణః సుకృతస్యాహుః సాత్త్వికం నిర్మలం ఫలమ్ ।
రజసస్తు ఫలం దుఃఖమ్  అజ్ఞానం తమసః ఫలమ్ ।। 16 ।।
translation_en: The fruits of deeds done in Sattva Guna give holy results. Actions done in Rajo Guna cause sorrows, and actions done in Tamo Guna cause darkness of ignorance.
explanation_en: Actions performed under sattva yield pure results, under rajas yield suffering, and under tamas yield further ignorance — this verse makes explicit that the gunas don't just describe inner states, they actively determine the character of whatever a person's actions produce.

sanskrit_sloka:
సత్త్వాత్ సంజాయతే జ్ఞానం రజసో లోభ ఏవ చ ।
ప్రమాదమోహౌ తమసో భవతోఽజ్ఞానమేవ చ ।। 17 ।।
translation_en: Sattva gives rise to knowledge, Rajo gives rise to greed (greed), and tamo gives rise to indifference and lust (delusion).
explanation_en: Sattva gives rise to knowledge, rajas to greed, tamas to negligence and delusion — restating the causal chain in slightly different terms reinforces the pattern: whichever guna a person feeds through habit and attention tends to generate more of its characteristic fruit.

translation_en: Those who are in sattva go to the upper worlds; Those who are in the Rajo Guna remain in the middle (of the worlds); Those who dwell in their own nature are degraded.
explanation_en: Describing sattva-dominant beings as ascending, rajas-dominant beings as remaining in the middle, and tamas-dominant beings as descending gives a spatial, almost gravitational metaphor for how these inner qualities translate into an overall trajectory across lifetimes.

translation_en: Whenever the wise know that in all actions, these tri-gunas are done and there is nothing else, and know that I am beyond these - they attain my divine nature.
explanation_en: The wise, Krishna says, recognize that all action is simply the gunas acting upon each other, and understanding themselves as beyond these three qualities, attain his own nature — the entire preceding analysis of the gunas culminates here in a specific kind of self-recognition that transcends the whole system just described.

translation_en: By transcending the trigunas of physical nature, one is freed from the miseries of birth, death and old age and attains immortality.
explanation_en: Transcending the three gunas is tied directly to freedom from birth, death, old age, and their accompanying suffering — the promise isn't just intellectual understanding of the gunas, but liberation from the very cycle their interplay had been driving.

translation_en: Arjuna asked: What are the characteristics of one who is beyond the tri-gunas of nature, O Lord? How do they behave? How do they become beyond the bonds of tri-gunas?
explanation_en: Arjuna's question — what does someone beyond the gunas actually look like, how do they behave, how is this transcendence reached — shifts from theory to practice, echoing his earlier question in chapter 2 about the person of steady wisdom. translation_en: Sri Bhagavan spoke: O Arjuna, those who are beyond these trigunas - neither hate (born in sattva guna) light, (born in rajo guna) activity, nor (born in tamo guna) delusion - when they are abundant, nor do they desire them when they are absent. They are neutral and indifferent to the qualities of nature and are not disturbed by them. Knowing that the gunas are acting, they remain still in the soul.
explanation_en: Krishna's answer describes someone who doesn't resent the presence of light, activity, or delusion when they arise, nor crave them when absent — a remarkably even-handed stance toward all three qualities, neither favoring the pleasant sattva nor rejecting the others outright.

translation_en: Those who serve Me through pure devotion transcend the trigunas of nature and reach the level of Brahman.
explanation_en: Pure, unwavering devotion is named here as the specific route that carries a person beyond the gunas entirely, reaching the level of Brahman — after all the analytical breakdown of sattva, rajas, and tamas, the actual path offered isn't more analysis but devotion.

translation_en: I am the basis of that eternal, immutable formless Brahman, eternal Dharma and infinite divine bliss.
explanation_en: The chapter's closing claim — that Krishna is the very foundation of the eternal, formless Brahman, of everlasting dharma, and of unlimited bliss — folds the entire preceding discussion of nature's three qualities back into a single source, positioning devotion to him as ultimately inseparable from Brahman itself.

ఊర్ధ్వమూలమధః శాఖమశ్వత్థం  ప్రాహురవ్యయమ్ ।

translation_en: Sri Bhagavanu Palikenu: It is said about the Asvattha Vriksha which is an orthodox tree with roots upwards and branches downwards. Its leaves are Vedic mantras, and those who know the secret of this tree know the Vedas.
explanation_en: The image of a tree with roots above and branches below is deliberately disorienting — trees don't grow that way, and that's the point. translation_en: Nourished by the tri-gunas, the branches of this tree, extending up and down, sense objects are like gums to them. For karma to flow in human form, the roots of the tree are rooted downwards. Below, its roots spread out into branches, causing karma in the human world.
explanation_en: Describing the branches as nourished by the three gunas, extending both upward and downward, with roots reaching further down into the human world where they generate action, maps the whole structure of worldly involvement onto this single, sprawling tree — one continuous system, not separate compartments of life.

తమేవ చాద్యం  పురుషం  ప్రపద్యే

translation_en: The real nature of this tree is not known in this world, nor is its beginning, end or orthodox existence understood. But, this deep-rooted tree of indifference must be cut down by the strong ax of apathy/vairagya. Then the beginning of that tree should be sought, that is God, from whom the production of this world took place long ago. After taking refuge in Him, we will not enter this world again.
explanation_en: Krishna's admission that this tree's true form, beginning, and end aren't understood in the ordinary world sets up the instruction that follows: since the tree can't simply be studied and outgrown through observation, it needs to be actively cut down with what he calls the strong axe of detachment.

translation_en: Those who are free from avarice and lust, who have conquered lust, who are eternally in the mind of God, who have no desire to experience sensual pleasures, who are beyond pleasures, sorrows and dualities - such liberated beings attain my Parampada.
explanation_en: The description of those free from pride and delusion, who've conquered attachment and remain constantly absorbed in the divine, reads like a composite portrait built from qualities scattered across earlier chapters — this verse gathers them together as the profile of someone who has actually reached the goal.

translation_en: Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor the fire can illuminate my supreme abode. People who went there never return to this physical world.
explanation_en: Claiming that Krishna's supreme abode needs no illumination from sun, moon, or fire — and that no one returns from it once reached — describes a destination fundamentally unlike any place lit by ordinary means. It isn't brighter than the physical world; it operates by an entirely different kind of light.

sanskrit_sloka:

translation_en: The living souls in the material world are the eternal aspects of Me. But, bound by physical energy, they are struggling with the six senses which are connected with the mind.
explanation_en: Calling embodied souls 'eternal fragments' of Krishna himself, struggling against the mind and six senses, reframes ordinary human difficulty in startling terms — the very struggle people experience daily is described as a fragment of the divine caught in friction with its own borrowed instruments of perception.

translation_en: Just as the wind carries the fragrance from one place to another, so the soul, leaving the old body and entering the new body, takes the mind and senses along with it.
explanation_en: The image of wind carrying fragrance from place to place gives real texture to how the soul is described as moving from one body to the next, taking mind and senses along — not vanishing at death, but transferring, the way scent travels without needing to be seen doing so.

translation_en: With the perception of the sense organs - ears, eyes, skin, tongue and nose - which are dependent on the mind, the living soul enjoys the sense objects.
explanation_en: Listing the specific senses — ear, eye, skin, tongue, nose — through which the soul engages with its objects grounds the previous verse's abstract image of transference in something concrete: this is how the soul actually experiences a body, one sense channel at a time, once it arrives.

sanskrit_sloka:

translation_en: Ignorant people do not notice the Jivatman - either when it is in the body enjoying sense objects or when it leaves the body. But those with wise eyes can see it.
explanation_en: The claim that most people fail to notice the soul either while it inhabits a body or when it departs, while the wise can perceive it, locates a real perceptual gap at the heart of ordinary experience — something Krishna insists is happening constantly, yet remains invisible to untrained attention.

sanskrit_sloka:
యతంతో  యోగినశ్చైనం  పశ్యంత్యాత్మన్యవస్థితమ్ ।
యతంతోఽప్యకృతాత్మానో  నైనం పశ్యంత్యచేతసః  ।। 11 ।।
translation_en: Even the assiduous yogis are able to know the soul residing in the body. But, no matter how hard they try, those who are not purified in the inner world will not be able to know it.
explanation_en: Even dedicated practitioners, Krishna admits, struggle to perceive the soul clearly if their inner world isn't sufficiently purified — a candid acknowledgment that effort alone doesn't guarantee this particular kind of insight; the instrument of perception itself has to be refined first.

sanskrit_sloka:
యదాదిత్యగతం  తేజో  జగద్భాసయతేఽఖిలమ్  ।
యచ్చంద్రమసి  యాచ్చాగ్నౌ తత్తేజో  విద్ధి మామకమ్  ।। 12 ।।
translation_en: Know that I am the effulgence of the sun that illuminates the entire solar system. Know that the radiance of the moon and the light of fire emanate from me.
explanation_en: Naming himself as the radiance of the sun that lights the entire solar system, and the source of the moon and fire's glow as well, extends the same logic from chapter 10's catalog into a tighter focus specifically on light — every visible source of illumination is claimed as originating in him.

translation_en: Pervading and pervading the earth, I nourish all beings by My energy. Being the moon, I nourish all the plants.
explanation_en: Describing himself as entering the earth and sustaining all beings through his energy, nourishing plants specifically as the moon, ties cosmic claims back down to the very practical business of growth and sustenance — the divine isn't only lofty and distant, it's active in soil and rainfall and moonlight.

translation_en: I assume the form of Jatharagni, the soul-drinking soul in the stomachs of living beings, to digest and digest the four kinds of food.
explanation_en: The claim to become the digestive fire within living beings, breaking down the four kinds of food, is among the most physically intimate images in the whole text — divinity located not in some abstract height but in the literal biological process happening inside every eating creature.

వేదైశ్చ సర్వైరహమేవ  వేద్యో

translation_en: I am present in the hearts of all beings, and from Me arise memory, knowledge, and forgetfulness. I am the only one to be known through all the Vedas, I am the author of Vedanta, and I am the knower of Vedardha.
explanation_en: Present in every heart as the source of memory, knowledge, and forgetting alike, and named as both the object of all Vedic knowledge and its author, Krishna claims responsibility for the entire spectrum of mental experience — not just what people remember and understand, but what they lose track of too.

sanskrit_sloka:
ద్వావిమౌ పురుషౌ లోకే క్షరశ్చాక్షర  ఏవ చ ।

translation_en: There are two types of living beings in creation, Ksharams (perishable) and Aksharmas (imperishable). All that exists in the physical world is alkali. Aksharams are beings who have attained salvation.
explanation_en: Dividing all beings into the perishable and the imperishable — everything in the material world falling into the first category, liberated beings into the second — gives a clean two-part taxonomy that the next verse will immediately complicate by introducing something beyond both.

translation_en: Besides these, there is that Purushottam, the imperishable Supreme Soul. He enters the universe as the eternal God and sustains all living beings.
explanation_en: Introducing Purushottama, the imperishable Supreme Soul who enters and sustains the universe while remaining distinct from it, adds a third category beyond the perishable and imperishable already named — not a midpoint between them, but something that encompasses and exceeds both.

translation_en: He who knows me without doubt as the Supreme Purushotta, has perfect knowledge. O Arjuna, they worship me wholeheartedly.
explanation_en: Knowing Krishna without doubt as this Supreme Person is called complete knowledge here, and the response to that knowledge, wholehearted worship, follows almost as a natural consequence — right understanding and devoted response are presented as tightly linked, not separate accomplishments.

ఏతద్ బుద్ధ్వా బుద్ధిమాన్ స్యాత్ కృతకృత్యశ్చ భారత  ।। 20 ।।

translation_en: Sri Bhagavanu Palikenu: O descendant of Bharata, these are the qualities of a person of divine wealth - fearlessness, untainted mind, determination in spiritual knowledge, charity, restraint of senses, performance of sacrifices, recitation of holy scriptures, penance and openness; non-violence, truthfulness, non-anger, self-sacrifice, peace, non-fault-finding, kindness to all living beings, non-covetousness, gentleness, modesty and stillness; Strength, forgiveness, equanimity, cleanliness, no enmity towards anyone and no hypocrisy.
explanation_en: The list opening this chapter — fearlessness, purity of mind, charity, self-control — reads almost like a job description for a fully realized person, and starting with fearlessness specifically suggests it's foundational: hard to practice genuine generosity or restraint from a place of anxiety.

దానం దమశ్చ యజ్ఞశ్చ స్వాధ్యాయస్తప ఆర్జవమ్ ।। 1 ।।', 'అహింసా సత్యమక్రోధః \xa0త్యాగః శాంతిరపైశునమ్ ।
దయా భూతేష్వలోలుప్త్వం మార్దవం హ్రీరచాపలమ్ ।। 2 ।।', 'తేజః క్షమా ధృతిః శౌచమద్రోహో నాతిమానితా ।
భవంతి సంపదం దైవీమభిజాతస్య భారత ।। 3 ।।']
translation_en: Sri Bhagavanu Palikenu: O descendant of Bharata, these are the qualities of a person of divine wealth - fearlessness, untainted mind, determination in spiritual knowledge, charity, restraint of senses, performance of sacrifices, recitation of holy scriptures, penance and openness; non-violence, truthfulness, non-anger, self-sacrifice, peace, non-fault-finding, kindness to all living beings, non-covetousness, gentleness, modesty and stillness; Strength, forgiveness, equanimity, cleanliness, no enmity towards anyone and no hypocrisy.
explanation_en: The list's final stretch — strength, forgiveness, cleanliness, freedom from hypocrisy — closes with qualities that require real inner consistency, matching outward behavior to inward state. Ending on 'no hypocrisy' feels deliberate, as if summarizing that the whole list only counts if it's genuine, not performed.

sanskrit_sloka:
దంభో దర్పోఽభిమానశ్చ  క్రోధః  పారుష్యమేవ  చ  ।
అజ్ఞానం చాభిజాతస్య పార్థ  సంపదమాసురీమ్  ।। 4 ।।
translation_en: O Partha, arrogance, arrogance, pride, anger, rudeness, and ignorance are the qualities of those with demonic nature.
explanation_en: By contrast, the demonic list is short and blunt: arrogance, pride, anger, harshness, ignorance. There's no attempt to make this list feel sympathetic or nuanced — Krishna presents it almost as a warning label, naming the cluster of traits to actively avoid without hedging.

sanskrit_sloka:
దైవీ సంపద్విమోక్షాయ నిబంధాయాసురీ మతా ।
మా శుచః సంపదం దైవీమభిజాతోఽసి పాండవ ।। 5 ।।
translation_en: Divine qualities lead to salvation, but demonic qualities cause one to remain trapped in bondage. Don't worry Arjuna, you were born with divine qualities.
explanation_en: Reassuring Arjuna directly that he was born with divine qualities is a notably personal aside within an otherwise general teaching — Krishna isn't just cataloging abstract types, he's telling Arjuna specifically which category he belongs to, addressing an anxiety Arjuna hasn't even voiced yet.

sanskrit_sloka:
ద్వౌ భూతసర్గౌ లోకేఽస్మిన్  దైవ ఆసుర ఏవ చ ।
దైవో విస్తరశః ప్రోక్త ఆసురం పార్థ మే శృణు ।। 6 ।।
translation_en: There are two types of beings in this world - those with divine qualities and those with asura nature. I have elaborately described the divine qualities, O Arjuna, I will tell you about the nature of the Asuras, listen.
explanation_en: Dividing all beings into two basic natures — divine and demonic — before elaborating on the demonic type gives the chapter its structure: having spent several verses on the positive qualities, Krishna now turns deliberately toward describing their opposite in detail.

sanskrit_sloka:
ప్రవృత్తిం చ నివృత్తిం చ జనా న విదురాసురాః ।
న శౌచం నాపి చాచారో న సత్యం తేషు విద్యతే ।। 7 ।।
translation_en: Those with asura qualities do not understand what is good conduct and what is bad conduct. That is why they are not chaste, or virtuous, or at least truthful.
explanation_en: Describing those of demonic nature as unable to distinguish right conduct from wrong locates the core problem not in bad choices exactly, but in a kind of broken perception — the moral compass itself, not just individual decisions, is described as malfunctioning.

sanskrit_sloka:
అసత్యమప్రతిష్ఠం తే జగదాహురనీశ్వరమ్ ।
అపరస్పరసంభూతం కిమన్యత్ కామహైతుకమ్ ।। 8 ।।
translation_en: They say, "There is no absolute truth in this world, no basis (of moral code), and no God (who created or maintains it). It all originates from male-female union and serves no other purpose than sexual gratification."  that
explanation_en: The demonic worldview as Krishna summarizes it — no absolute truth, no moral foundation, no God, existence reduced to reproduction without further purpose — reads like a compressed philosophical nihilism, stripped of any larger meaning beyond immediate biological function.

sanskrit_sloka:
ఏతాం దృష్టిమవష్టభ్య నష్టాత్మానోఽల్పబుద్ధయః ।
ప్రభవంతి ఉగ్రకర్మాణః క్షయాయ జగతోఽహితాః ।। 9 ।।
translation_en: Firmly held in such a view, these misguided souls, with low intelligence and violent deeds, become enemies of the world and threaten to destroy it.
explanation_en: Holding this view firmly, Krishna says, leads people with limited understanding into destructive action, becoming enemies of the world. The claim connects a philosophical position directly to real-world harm — ideas, in this framing, aren't neutral, they shape what people are willing to do.

sanskrit_sloka:
కామమాశ్రిత్య దుష్పూరం దంభమానమదాన్వితాః ।
మోహాద్గృహీత్వాసద్గ్రాహాన్ ప్రవర్తంతేఽశుచివ్రతాః ।। 10 ।।
translation_en: Filled with excessive lust, arrogance, avarice, pride and arrogance, these asura-characteristics hold false doctrines. Thus enamored, they are attracted to temporal things and act with an impure mind.
explanation_en: Driven by insatiable desire, arrogance, and false pride, holding onto wrong beliefs out of delusion, such people are drawn to impermanent things and act from impure motives — the picture builds a feedback loop where wrong belief and wrong desire continually reinforce each other.

sanskrit_sloka:
చింతామపరిమేయాం చ ప్రలయాంతాముపాశ్రితాః ।

translation_en: Their endless worry-worries ultimately end in death. However, they are convinced that the gratification of desires and the accumulation of wealth is the ultimate goal of life.
explanation_en: Consumed by endless anxiety that only ends at death, yet still convinced that sensual gratification and wealth accumulation are life's ultimate purpose — there's a real tragedy embedded in this description: a lifetime of worry spent chasing a goal that never actually delivers the peace it promises.

translation_en: Bound by hundreds of desires, and beset by lustful wraths, they labor to amass wealth in unrighteous ways, all for the sake of their sensual pleasures.
explanation_en: Bound by hundreds of desires, driven by lust and anger, laboring to accumulate wealth through unrighteous means purely for sensory pleasure — the specificity of 'hundreds of desires' emphasizes not just wanting things, but being genuinely overwhelmed and directed by the sheer volume of craving.

యక్ష్యే దాస్యామి మోదిష్య ఇత్యజ్ఞానవిమోహితాః ।। 15 ।।']
translation_en: Those with asura qualities think, "I have already acquired a lot of money today, I will fulfill this desire of mine. All this is mine, tomorrow I will still have it. That enemy is destroyed by me, I will destroy others too! I myself am like God, I am the one who indulges all this, I am powerful and I am comfortable. I am rich and my relatives are in great position. Who is my equal? I offer sacrifices (to the gods)." I will do; I will give alms; I will enjoy." Thus, they become enamored by ignorance.
explanation_en: The extended internal monologue Krishna voices — 'I have gained this, I will gain that, this enemy I've destroyed, I'll destroy others too' — is remarkable for how recognizable it sounds, giving demonic thinking a specific, almost conversational interior voice rather than an abstract category.

explanation_en: Blinded by ego, power, pride, lust, and anger, such people harbor resentment toward the divine presence within themselves and others — the demonic disposition, in its final development, turns hostile not just to abstract principle but to the divine wherever it's actually encountered.

sanskrit_sloka: ['తానహం ద్విషతః క్రూరాన్ సంసారేషు నరాధమాన్ ।\nక్షిపామ్యజస్రమశుభానాసురీష్వేవ యోనిషు ।। 19 ।।', 'ఆసురీం యోనిమాపన్నా మూఢా జన్మని జన్మని ।\nమామప్రాప్యైవ కౌంతేయ తతో యాంత్యధమాం గతిమ్ ।। 20 ।।']
translation_en: I, in the cycle of rebirth of the material world, repeatedly cast into the wombs of such demonic natures, evil and hateful in nature. These foolish souls are born again and again in the Asura wombs. Unable to reach Me, O Arjuna, they gradually fall into the lowest state of existence.
explanation_en: Krishna's statement that he repeatedly casts such natures into demonic wombs across the cycle of rebirth introduces real consequence beyond a single lifetime — not as arbitrary punishment, but as the natural continuation of a pattern that hasn't been interrupted.

sanskrit_sloka:
త్రివిధం నరకస్యేదం ద్వారం నాశనమాత్మనః  ।
కామః క్రోధస్తథా లోభస్తస్మాదేతత్త్రయం త్యజేత్  ।। 21 ।।
translation_en: There are three gates of hell that lead to the destruction of the soul - lust, anger, and greed. So, everyone should leave these.
explanation_en: Naming lust, anger, and greed as the three gates of hell that destroy the soul gives Arjuna something concrete and memorable — after pages describing the demonic personality in elaborate detail, the chapter distills the actual entry points down to just three specific forces.

sanskrit_sloka:
ఏతైర్విముక్తః కౌంతేయ తమోద్వారైః త్రిభిర్నరః ।

translation_en: Those who are freed from these three gates of darkness, strive for the well-being of the soul, so that they attain the ultimate goal.
explanation_en: Freedom from these three gates is described as opening the way to genuine well-being and the ultimate goal — a hopeful counterpoint immediately following the stark warning, showing the exit is as clearly identified as the trap itself.

sanskrit_sloka:

న స సిద్ధిమవాప్నోతి న సుఖం న పరాం గతిమ్ ।। 23 ।।
translation_en: Those who do not follow the instructions given in the Shastra, but are motivated by lust, they cannot achieve perfect Siddhi, happiness, and ultimately the ultimate goal of life.
explanation_en: Those who abandon scriptural guidance, acting instead purely from personal desire, are said to fail at happiness, perfection, and the ultimate goal — a warning less about disobedience for its own sake and more about the practical consequence of navigating by craving alone.

sanskrit_sloka:
తస్మాచ్ఛాస్త్రం ప్రమాణంతే కార్యాకార్యవ్యవస్థితౌ ।
జ్ఞాత్వా శాస్త్రవిధానోక్తం కర్మ కర్తుమిహార్హసి ।। 24 ।।
translation_en: So, let's take science as the standard of what to do and what not to do. Learn the rules and teachings of science and act accordingly in this world.
explanation_en: The chapter's closing instruction — let scripture be the standard for determining right and wrong action — offers a concrete resolution to everything just described: rather than trusting personal impulse, which the chapter has shown can drift disastrously astray, an external, tested reference point is recommended instead.

sanskrit_sloka:
అర్జున ఉవాచ ।
యే శాస్త్రవిధిముత్సృజ్య యజంతే శ్రద్దయాన్వితాః ।
తేషాం నిష్ఠా తు కా కృష్ణ సత్వమాహో రజస్తమః ।। 1 ।।
translation_en: Arjuna said: O Krishna, what is the condition of those who renounce (neglect) the duties of science and yet worship with devotion? Is their faith in Sattva Guna or Rajo and Tamo Gunas?
explanation_en: Arjuna's question about people who abandon scriptural procedure yet still worship with sincere devotion is genuinely tricky — it probes the gap between the previous chapter's insistence on scripture as the standard and the obvious reality that plenty of sincere people worship without following it precisely.

sanskrit_sloka:
శ్రీ భగవానువాచ ।
త్రివిధా భవతి శ్రద్ధా దేహినాం సా స్వభావజా ।
సాత్త్వికీ రాజసీ చైవ తామసీ చేతి తాం శృణు ।। 2 ।।
translation_en: Sri Bhagavan said: Every human being is born with his innate devotion/faith, which may be of three types - sattvik, rajas, or tamas. Now hear from me on this matter.
explanation_en: Krishna's response — that everyone is born with an innate faith shaped by one of the three gunas — reframes the question before answering it directly. Faith itself, it turns out, isn't uniform or automatically pure; it comes pre-colored by the same three qualities running through everything else.

sanskrit_sloka:
సత్త్వానురూపా సర్వస్య శ్రద్ధా భవతి భారత ।

translation_en: All men have beliefs according to the nature of their mind. Everyone has beliefs, and what they believe is their personality.
explanation_en: Stating plainly that a person's beliefs match the nature of their mind, and that what they believe essentially constitutes who they are, makes an unusually strong claim: faith isn't separate from character, it's practically identical to it — a person becomes, in some sense, what they believe.

sanskrit_sloka:

translation_en: Those in sattva guna worship the gods; Those in Rajoguna worship Yakshas and Rakshasas; Those in the Tamo Guna worship ghosts.
explanation_en: Sorting worship itself by guna — the sattvic worshipping gods, the rajasic worshipping powerful spirits, the tamasic worshipping ghosts — extends the three-fold framework into religious practice itself. Even sincere devotion, Krishna suggests, can be shaped and limited by which quality dominates the worshipper.

sanskrit_sloka: ['అశాస్త్రవిహితం ఘోరం తప్యంతే యే తపో జనాః ।\nదంభాహంకారసంయుక్తాః కామరాగబలాన్వితాః ।। 5 ।।', 'కర్షయంతః శరీరస్థం భూతగ్రామమచేతసః ।\nమాం చైవాంతః శరీరస్థం తాన్ విద్ధ్యాసురనిశ్చయాన్ ।। 6 ।।']

Driven by lust and lust, they afflict not only their bodily organs but also Me, who is the Supreme Soul, within their bodies. Know that such mindless people are of asura nature.
explanation_en: Describing severe, unscientific austerities performed out of vanity and pride as harmful not just to the practitioner's own body but to the divine presence within them adds real weight to the warning — self-punishment disguised as discipline doesn't just fail to help, it's described as actively injurious.

sanskrit_sloka:
ఆహారస్త్వపి సర్వస్య త్రివిధో భవతి ప్రియః ।
యజ్ఞస్తపస్తథా దానం తేషాం భేదమిమం శృణు ।। 7 ।।
translation_en: People's food preferences depend on their nature.  Yajnas, penance, and charity also depend on their disposition. Now listen to these differences.
explanation_en: Extending the three-guna framework into food preferences might seem like a strange pivot after such weighty spiritual material, but it signals something important: these qualities aren't confined to abstract belief, they show up in the most ordinary daily choices, starting with what a person eats.

sanskrit_sloka:
ఆయుః సత్త్వబలారోగ్యసుఖప్రీతివివర్ధనాః ।
రస్యాః స్నిగ్ధాః స్థిరా హృద్యా ఆహారాః సాత్త్వికప్రియాః ।। 8 ।।
translation_en: Virtue-dominant – likes things that increase longevity, and promote comfort, strength, health, happiness, and contentment. Such foods are juicy, nutritious, nutritious, and naturally delicious.
explanation_en: Foods associated with sattva — nourishing, naturally flavorful, promoting health and contentment — are described in terms of what they build up rather than what they excite, matching sattva's broader character throughout the text as the quality oriented toward stability and genuine wellbeing.

sanskrit_sloka:
కట్వమ్లలవణాత్యుష్ణతీక్ష్ణరూక్షవిదాహినః  ।
ఆహారా రాజసస్యేష్టా  దుఃఖశోకామయప్రదాః  ।। 9 ।।
translation_en: Foods that are very bitter, very sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry and spicy are preferred by those with Rajo guna predominance. Such foods cause suffering, grief and disease.
explanation_en: Rajasic food — bitter, sour, excessively spiced, causing discomfort and disease — mirrors rajas's broader association with intensity and restlessness; the food itself agitates the body the way rajasic activity agitates the mind, extending the pattern down to something as basic as taste.

sanskrit_sloka:
యాతయామం గతరసం పూతి పర్యుషితం చ యత్ ।
ఉచ్ఛిష్టమపి చామేధ్యం భోజనం తామసప్రియమ్ ।। 10 ।।
translation_en: Dried/spoilt food, rotten food, contaminated and impure food – are dear to those who have Tamasi Guna as their predominance.
explanation_en: Tamasic food — stale, spoiled, impure — completes the pattern at its lowest register: not stimulating like rajasic food, but simply degraded, matching tamas's association throughout the text with decay, inertia, and neglect rather than active harm.

sanskrit_sloka:
అఫలాకాంక్షిభిర్యజ్ఞో విధిదృష్టో య ఇజ్యతే ।
యష్టవ్యమేవేతి మనః సమాధాయ స సాత్త్వికః ।। 11 ।।
translation_en: It is as if the yajna performed with sattva guna is performed with a firm determination in the mind that this is the duty to be done, following the rules of science without any desire for results.
explanation_en: A sattvic sacrifice, performed with firm resolve simply because it's the right thing to do, without craving any particular result, defines the purest form of ritual action — not by its scale or intensity, but by the complete absence of self-interested motive behind it.

sanskrit_sloka:
అభిసంధాయ తు ఫలం దంభార్థమపి చైవ యత్ ।
ఇజ్యతే భరతశ్రేష్ఠ తం యజ్ఞం విద్ధి రాజసమ్ ।। 12 ।।
translation_en: O great Bharata, know that a yajna for worldly gain or pride is in Rajoguna.
explanation_en: A rajasic sacrifice, performed for worldly gain or personal pride, keeps the same outward form as its sattvic counterpart but corrupts it from within — the difference isn't visible in the ritual itself but in what the performer is actually hoping to get out of it.

sanskrit_sloka:
విధిహీనమసృష్టాన్నం మంత్రహీనమదక్షిణమ్ ।
శ్రద్ధావిరహితం యజ్ఞం తామసం పరిచక్షతే ।। 13 ।।
translation_en: A yajna performed without devotion and contrary to the rules of Shastra, without distribution of prasada, chanting of mantras, and without giving Dakshina, is considered to be of Tamo Guna.
explanation_en: A tamasic sacrifice, performed without devotion, disregarding scriptural procedure, skipping the distribution of offerings and proper payment to officiants, describes ritual reduced to careless motion — going through gestures without any of the substance that would make them meaningful.
word_by_word_meaning_en: vidhi-hinam — not the teaching of science; asrishta-annam — without distribution of prasada; mantra-hinam — without chanting Vedic mantras; adakshinam — without giving dakshina to the priests;  sraddha viraivam — without attention; Yajna — Yajna; tamasam — in tamoguna; Parikkshate — Considered.

sanskrit_sloka:
దేవద్విజగురుప్రాజ్ఞపూజనం శౌచమార్జవమ్ ।
బ్రహ్మచర్యమహింసా చ శారీరం తప ఉచ్యతే ।। 14 ।।
translation_en: Worship of the Supreme Lord, Brahmins, spiritual master, sages and elders - whenever it is done while practicing purity, chastity, celibacy and non-violence - is said to be physical penance.
explanation_en: Physical penance, defined here as reverence toward the divine, elders, and teachers, practiced alongside purity, celibacy, and non-violence, ties bodily discipline directly to relational respect — restraint of the body isn't isolated self-control, it's bound up with how one treats others.

sanskrit_sloka:
అనుద్వేగకరం వాక్యం సత్యం ప్రియహితం చ యత్ ।
స్వాధ్యాయాభ్యసనం చైవ వాజ్ఞ్మయం తప ఉచ్యతే ।। 15 ।।
translation_en: Speech that does not cause emotion, truths, that does not cause anger, beloved things and recitation of eternal Vedic scriptures - these are said to be verbal penance.
explanation_en: Verbal penance — speech that doesn't wound, that's truthful, pleasant, and rooted in study of scripture — sets a demanding standard: not just avoiding lies, but avoiding even truthful speech delivered in a way that causes unnecessary pain.
word_by_word_meaning_en: anudvega-karam — non-emotional; vakaya — words; satyam — truths; priya-hitam — useful/beneficial; Cha — and; yat — whatever;  svadhyaya-abhyasana — study of the Vedic sciences; cha eva — and yet; vajnmayam — relating to speech; tapa — penance; Uchyate — shall be stated.

sanskrit_sloka:
మనః ప్రసాదః సౌమ్యత్వం మౌనమాత్మవినిగ్రహః ।
భావసంశుద్ధిరిత్యేతత్ తపో మానసముచ్యతే ।। 16 ।।
translation_en: Calmness of thought, gentleness, silence, self-restraint and purity of feeling - all these are known as penance of the mind.
explanation_en: Mental penance — calmness, gentleness, silence, self-control, purity of thought — completes the three-tiered picture of discipline across body, speech, and mind, suggesting genuine penance has to reach all three levels rather than stopping at outward behavior alone.
word_by_word_meaning_en: manah prasadah — tranquility of mind; gentleness — to be gentle; Maunam — silence; atma-vinigrahah — restraint of the soul; bhava-samshuddhih — purity in feeling; iti — in this way; etat — all these; tapah — penance; manasam — of the mind; uchyate — what is said.

sanskrit_sloka:
శ్రద్ధయా పరయా తప్తం తపస్తత్ త్రివిధం  నరైః  ।
అఫలాకాంక్షిభిర్యుక్తైః  సాత్త్వికం పరిచక్షతే  ।। 17 ।।
translation_en: If these three penances are practiced with great faith by the pious devotees without any expectation of material rewards, they are called sattvic penances.
explanation_en: Practicing these three forms of penance with deep faith and no expectation of reward is what qualifies them as sattvic — the same emphasis on motive over form that ran through the discussion of sacrifice now applies equally to austerity.

sanskrit_sloka:
సత్కారమానపూజార్థం తపో దంభేన చైవ యత్ ।
క్రియతే తదిహ ప్రోక్తం రాజసం చలమధ్రువమ్ ।। 18 ।।
translation_en: For glory, honour, and magnanimity, ostentatious austerities/yagnas are in Rajo Guna. Its benefits are transient, and temporary.
explanation_en: Penance performed for the sake of recognition, honor, or being admired is named rajasic here, and its results are described as fleeting and unstable — the effort might look identical to genuine discipline from outside, but what it produces doesn't last.

sanskrit_sloka:
మూఢగ్రాహేణాత్మనో యత్పీడయా క్రియతే తపః ।
పరస్యోత్సాదనార్థం వా తత్తామసముదాహృతమ్ ।। 19 ।।
translation_en: Penance done with confused feelings, torturing oneself or harming others, is said to be in the nature of tamo.
explanation_en: Penance carried out with confused understanding, involving self-torture or harm to others, is called tamasic — closing the loop with the earlier warning in verse 5 about austerity practiced from ego rather than genuine spiritual aspiration.

sanskrit_sloka:
దాతవ్యమితి యద్దానం దీయతేఽనుపకారిణే ।
దేశే కాలే చ పాత్రే చ తద్దానం సాత్త్వికం స్మృతమ్ ।। 20 ।।
translation_en: Giving alms is said to be sattvaguna dana if one considers it a duty (right thing to do) and gives alms at the right time and in the right place, without any reward.
explanation_en: Sattvic charity is defined as giving simply because it's the right thing to do, offered at the appropriate time and place, without any expectation of return — the same pattern of pure motive determining quality that has run through sacrifice, penance, and now giving as well.

sanskrit_sloka:
యత్తు ప్రత్యుపకారార్థం ఫలముద్దిశ్య వా పునః ।
దీయతే చ పరిక్లిష్టం తద్ధానం రాజసం స్మృతమ్ ।। 21 ।।
translation_en: Donation given reluctantly, with the hope of something in return or with the expectation of a reward, is said to be in Rajo Guna.
explanation_en: Charity given reluctantly, or with hope of some benefit in return, is called rajasic — even generosity, it turns out, can be subtly transactional, and Krishna is precise about naming that subtlety rather than letting any act of giving pass as automatically virtuous.

sanskrit_sloka:
అదేశకాలే యద్ధానమ్ అపాత్రేభ్యశ్చ దీయతే ।
అసత్కృతమవజ్ఞాతం తత్తామసముదాహృతమ్ ।। 22 ।।
translation_en: Donation given at an inappropriate place, at an inappropriate time, to an undeserving (apatra), without courtesy, or carelessly, is considered tamasadana.
explanation_en: Charity given at the wrong time or place, to an unworthy recipient, without respect or care, is tamasic — carelessness itself, independent of the amount given, is enough to degrade the act, regardless of whatever material value the gift might carry.

sanskrit_sloka:
ఓం తత్సదితి  నిర్దేశో బ్రహ్మణస్త్రివిధః స్మృతః  ।
బ్రాహ్మణాస్తేన వేదాశ్చ యజ్ఞాశ్చ విహితాః  పురా ।। 23 ।।
translation_en: The words "Om Tat Sat" have been prescribed from the beginning of creation as indicative of Parabrahman. From them arose priests, sciences and yagnas.
explanation_en: Introducing the phrase 'Om Tat Sat' as designating the Supreme from the very beginning of creation, and as the source from which priests, scriptures, and sacrifices arose, shifts the chapter from classifying human action by guna toward naming something that stands entirely outside that three-part system.

sanskrit_sloka:
తస్మాద్ ఓం ఇత్యుదాహృత్య యజ్ఞదానతపఃక్రియాః ।
ప్రవర్తంతే విధానోక్తాః సతతం బ్రహ్మావాదినామ్ ।। 24 ।।
translation_en: So, in performing yajnas, in giving alms, in performing austerities - the Vedic vidus, following the Vedic injunctions, always begin by uttering the sound 'Om'.
explanation_en: The instruction to begin every sacrifice, act of charity, and penance with the sound 'Om,' following Vedic practice, gives this abstract phrase a concrete ritual application — a verbal marker consistently placed at the start of exactly the actions just spent the whole chapter classifying.

sanskrit_sloka:
తదిత్యనభిసంధాయ ఫలం యఙ్ఞతపఃక్రియాః ।
దానక్రియాశ్చ వివిధాః క్రియంతే మోక్షకాంక్షిభిః ।। 25 ।।
translation_en: Those who do not expect any counter-fruits, but seek to be freed from these material bonds, utter the word "tat" while performing penance, yajna, and charity.
explanation_en: Uttering 'Tat' while performing penance, sacrifice, or charity, specifically by those seeking liberation without any interest in results, ties this second syllable to the motive of release rather than reward — matching the pure, non-transactional quality repeatedly identified as sattvic throughout the chapter.

sanskrit_sloka: ['సద్భావే సాధుభావే చ సదిత్యేతత్ప్రయుజ్యతే ।\nప్రశస్తే కర్మణి తథా సచ్ఛబ్దః  పార్థ యుజ్యతే ।। 26 ।।', 'యజ్ఞే తపసి దానే చ స్థితిః  సదితి చోచ్యతే ।\nకర్మ చైవ తదర్థీయం సదిత్యేవాభిధీయతే ।। 27 ।।']
translation_en: The word "Sat" means - orthodox existence and auspiciousness. O Arjuna, it is also used to denote an auspicious action. The term "sat" also describes engaging in the practice of yajna, penance, and charity.  Therefore, any work with this purpose is called "Sat".
explanation_en: Defining 'Sat' as denoting real existence and goodness, used to mark auspicious action, extends the three-syllable formula into a final component — reality and virtue named together, as though the two were inseparable at this level of understanding.

sanskrit_sloka: ['సద్భావే సాధుభావే చ సదిత్యేతత్ప్రయుజ్యతే ।\nప్రశస్తే కర్మణి తథా సచ్ఛబ్దః  పార్థ యుజ్యతే ।। 26 ।।', 'యజ్ఞే తపసి దానే చ స్థితిః  సదితి చోచ్యతే ।\nకర్మ చైవ తదర్థీయం సదిత్యేవాభిధీయతే ।। 27 ।।']
translation_en: The word "Sat" means - orthodox existence and auspiciousness. O Arjuna, it is also used to denote an auspicious action. The term "sat" also describes engaging in the practice of yajna, penance, and charity.  Therefore, any work with this purpose is called "Sat".
explanation_en: The repeated explanation of 'Sat' as describing engagement in sacrifice, penance, and charity reinforces that this closing formula isn't separate from everything the chapter has been examining — it's the verbal seal placed on action already qualified as genuinely good.

sanskrit_sloka:
అశ్రద్ధయా హుతం దత్తం తపస్తప్తం కృతం చ యత్ ।
అసదిత్యుచ్యతే పార్థ న చ తత్ప్రేత్య నో ఇహ ।। 28 ।।
translation_en: O son of Pritha, donations and sacrifices done with ashradha are called "asat". They are of no use either in this world or in the Hereafter.
explanation_en: The chapter's closing warning — that offerings and sacrifices performed without faith are called 'asat' and are worthless in this life or beyond — returns forcefully to the theme that opened the chapter: without genuine faith behind it, even correctly performed ritual amounts to nothing at all.

sanskrit_sloka:
అర్జున ఉవాచ ।
సన్న్యాసస్య మహాబాహో తత్త్వమిచ్ఛామి వేదితుమ్ ।
త్యాగస్య చ హృషీకేశ పృథక్ కేశినిషూదన ।। 1 ।।
translation_en: Arjuna said: O great-armed Krishna, I want to know the nature of 'sannyasa' (renunciation of karma) and 'tyagama' (renunciation of the desire to enjoy the fruits of karma). O Hrishikesh, who desires to know the difference between them too, O Keshinishudana.
explanation_en: Arjuna's request to distinguish sannyasa from tyaga returns to a question that has quietly run under the entire dialogue since chapter 3 — after seventeen chapters of teaching, he wants the vocabulary itself finally clarified, as if sensing the whole conversation is about to be summarized.

sanskrit_sloka:
శ్రీ భగవానువాచ ।
కామ్యానాం కర్మణాం న్యాసం సన్న్యాసం కవయో విదుః ।
సర్వకర్మఫలత్యాగం ప్రాహుస్త్యాగం విచక్షణాః ।। 2 ।।
translation_en: Sri Bhagavan said: Sanyasama, said the sages, is the renunciation of desires-induced karma. Pundits say that giving up all the fruits of karma is sacrifice.
explanation_en: Krishna's opening definitions — sannyasa as giving up desire-driven action, tyaga as giving up the fruits of action — sound close enough to blur together, and that near-overlap is deliberate: the chapter is about to spend real effort distinguishing things that look almost identical on the surface.
word_by_word_meaning_en: Sri Bhagavanuvacha — Sri Bhagavanu Palikenu; kamyanam — having desires; karmanam — of karma; nyasa — renunciation; Sannyasa — as Sanyasamu (renunciation of karmas); kavayah — learned; viduh — understanding; sarva — all; karma-phala — of the fruits of karma; Sacrifice — giving up the desire to enjoy the fruits of karma; prahuh — what is said; Sacrifice — renunciation of the desire to enjoy the fruits of karma; vichakshana — the wise.

sanskrit_sloka:
త్యాజ్యం దోషవదిత్యేకే కర్మ ప్రాహుర్మనీషిణః ।
యజ్ఞదానతపఃకర్మ న త్యాజ్యమితి చాపరే ।। 3 ।।
translation_en: Some learned men say that all forms of karma are sinful and should be avoided, while others say that yajna, charity and penance should never be given up.
explanation_en: Citing a genuine disagreement among the learned — some saying all action is tainted and should be dropped, others insisting sacrifice, charity, and penance must never be abandoned — Krishna doesn't hide the fact that this is a live debate, not settled doctrine, before offering his own resolution.
word_by_word_meaning_en: tyajyam — that which is to be given up (to be relinquished); dosha-vat — faults; iti — that; ake — some; karma — karmas; prahuh — declares; manishinah — the learned; yajna — sacrifice; dana — charity; tapah — penance; karma — karmas; na tyajyam — should never leave; iti — in this way; Cha — and; Pare — Others.

sanskrit_sloka:
నిశ్చయం శృణు మే తత్ర త్యాగే భరతసత్తమ ।
త్యాగో హి పురుషవ్యాఘ్ర త్రివిధః సంప్రకీర్తితః ।। 4 ।।
translation_en: Now listen to my final decision on the subject of sacrifice, O Purushavyagraha, it is said that sacrifice is of three types.
explanation_en: Promising his 'final decision' on the matter gives real weight to what follows — after acknowledging genuine scholarly disagreement, Krishna signals he's about to cut through the ambiguity rather than simply adding one more opinion to the pile.

sanskrit_sloka:
యజ్ఞదానతపఃకర్మ న త్యాజ్యం కార్యమేవ తత్ ।
యజ్ఞో దానం తపశ్చైవ పావనాని మనీషిణామ్ ।। 5 ।।
translation_en: Karma related to yajna, almsgiving and austerities should never be renounced; They must be done. Indeed yajna, charity and penance sanctify even the wise.
explanation_en: Insisting that sacrifice, charity, and penance should never be abandoned, since they purify even the wise, closes off the more extreme renunciationist position mentioned in verse 3 — these aren't beginner's practices to be outgrown, they remain valuable even at advanced stages.

sanskrit_sloka:
ఏతాన్యపి తు కర్మాణి సంగం త్యక్త్వా ఫలాని చ ।
కర్తవ్యానీతి మే పార్థ నిశ్చితం మతముత్తమమ్ ।। 6 ।।
translation_en: These activities should be done without any desire for fruits and without any desire for reward. This is my absolute and supreme judgment, O Arjuna.
explanation_en: The qualifier — perform these without craving results or reward — matters as much as the instruction to keep performing them. Krishna isn't defending the actions themselves so much as defending a particular way of doing them, stripped of the usual transactional expectation.

sanskrit_sloka:
నియతస్య తు సన్న్యాసః కర్మణో నోపపద్యతే ।
మోహాత్తస్య పరిత్యాగస్తామసః పరికీర్తితః ।। 7 ।।
translation_en: One should never renounce one's prescribed duties. Such confusion sacrifice is called Tamasika sacrifice.
explanation_en: Calling the abandonment of one's prescribed duties out of confusion 'tamasic renunciation' names the lowest form of tyaga — not a spiritual accomplishment at all, but simple avoidance dressed up as detachment, motivated by delusion rather than genuine understanding.

sanskrit_sloka:
దుఃఖమిత్యేవ యత్కర్మ కాయక్లేశభయాత్యజేత్ ।
స కృత్వా రాజసం త్యాగం నైవ త్యాగఫలం లభేత్ ।। 8 ।।
translation_en: Rajo Guna Tyaga is the act of abandoning one's obligatory duties, thinking that they are difficult or causing physical discomfort. Such a sacrifice is never salutary and does not contribute to our elevation.
explanation_en: Rajasic renunciation — abandoning duty because it's difficult or physically uncomfortable — identifies a subtler trap: this looks more deliberate than the tamasic version, but the underlying motive is still avoidance of discomfort, not genuine release from attachment to outcome.

sanskrit_sloka:
కార్యమిత్యేవ యత్కర్మ నియతం క్రియతేఽర్జున ।
సంగం త్యక్త్వా ఫలం చైవ స త్యాగః సాత్త్వికో మతః  ।। 9 ।।
translation_en: Arjuna, whenever actions are performed in accordance with duty, and desire for fruit is renounced, it is called sattva guna sacrifice.
explanation_en: Sattvic renunciation, by contrast, means continuing to perform one's duty precisely because it's duty, while letting go of any desire for the result — the action itself doesn't change from the other two categories; what changes entirely is the inner motive behind continuing to do it.

sanskrit_sloka:
న ద్వేష్ట్యకుశలం కర్మ కుశలే నానుషజ్జతే ।
త్యాగీ సత్త్వసమావిష్టో మేధావీ ఛిన్నసంశయః ।। 10 ।।
translation_en: True sacrifices are those who do not try to avoid disliked tasks or wish for favorite/favorable tasks. They are virtuous and they have no doubts.
explanation_en: Describing the true renunciate as someone who neither avoids unpleasant tasks nor seeks out pleasant ones, free of doubt, completes the picture: real tyaga isn't about which tasks get done, it's about equanimity toward all of them regardless of preference.

sanskrit_sloka:
న హి దేహభృతా శక్యం త్యక్తుం కర్మాణ్యశేషతః ।
యస్తు కర్మఫలత్యాగీ స త్యాగీత్యభిధీయతే ।। 11 ।।
translation_en: It is not possible for any living being with a body to renounce karma completely. Hence, one who renounces the fruits of his karma is said to be a true sacrificer.
explanation_en: The observation that no embodied being can fully renounce action altogether — since even breathing and thinking are actions — grounds the whole discussion in practical reality. What's actually available to renounce is never action itself, only the craving for its fruit.

sanskrit_sloka:
అనిష్టమిష్టం మిశ్రం చ త్రివిధం కర్మణః ఫలమ్ ।
భవత్యత్యాగినాం ప్రేత్య న తు సన్న్యాసినాం క్వచిత్ ।। 12 ।।
translation_en: For those who are interested in self-interest, even the deceased Pidapa, - happiness, sorrow and a mixture of the two - will have karmic rewards in these three forms.  But, those who perform karmaphala sacrifice will not have such fruits either in this world or in the next world.
explanation_en: Contrasting those attached to results, who continue experiencing pleasant, unpleasant, and mixed karmic consequences, with those who've renounced the fruit and experience none of these consequences either now or later, gives the clearest statement yet of what's actually at stake in this distinction.

sanskrit_sloka:
పంచైతాని మహాబాహో కారణాని నిబోధ మే ।
సాంఖ్యే కృతాంతే ప్రోక్తాని సిద్దయే సర్వకర్మణామ్ ।। 13 ।।
translation_en: O Arjuna, listen now to what Samkhya Shastra says about the five factors behind any action, which explains how to prevent karmic reactions.
explanation_en: Introducing the five factors behind every action — as taught in Samkhya philosophy — shifts from moral classification toward mechanical analysis: Krishna is about to explain not just how actions should be evaluated, but literally how any action comes to happen at all.

sanskrit_sloka:
అధిష్ఠానం తథా కర్తా కరణం చ పృథగ్విధమ్ ।
వివిధాశ్చ పృథక్ చేష్టా దైవం చైవాత్ర పంచమమ్ ।। 14 ।।
translation_en: Body, Karta, various senses, various kinds of effort, divine grace - these are the five limbs of karma.
explanation_en: Naming the body, the individual doer, the various instruments (senses), the range of efforts, and divine will as the five components of any action distributes responsibility across multiple factors rather than locating it entirely in a single willing self — a person is only one piece of what produces any outcome.

sanskrit_sloka: ['శరీరవాఙ్మనోభిర్యత్ కర్మ ప్రారభతే నరః ।\nన్యాయ్యం వా విపరీతం వా పంచైతే తస్య హేతవః ।। 15 ।।', 'తత్రైవం సతి కర్తారమ్ ఆత్మానం కేవలం తు యః ।\nపశ్యత్యకృతబుద్ధిత్వాత్ న స పశ్యతి దుర్మతిః ।। 16 ।।']
translation_en: Whatever karma/deed done by the body, speech, mind, be it good or bad, these five are its factors. Those who do not understand this think that the soul is the real doer. Such people with impure mind cannot understand the reality.
explanation_en: Whatever action is performed through body, speech, or mind, whether right or wrong, involves these same five factors — and those who don't grasp this, believing the isolated self to be the sole doer, are said to see with an impure, incomplete understanding.

translation_en: Whatever karma/deed done by the body, speech, mind, be it good or bad, these five are its factors. Those who do not understand this think that the soul is the real doer. Such people with impure mind cannot understand the reality.

sanskrit_sloka:
యస్య నాహంకృతో భావో బుద్ధిర్యస్య న లిప్యతే ।
హత్వాఽపి  స ఇమాఁల్లోకాన్న హంతి న నిబధ్యతే  ।। 17 ।।
translation_en: Abandoning the sense of kartrutva ahamkara bhava (the sense that I am the doer) and whose intellect is disinterested, even if they kill living beings, they are not killed and become bound by karma.
explanation_en: The striking claim that someone free of ego, whose understanding isn't clouded, doesn't incur karmic bondage even while killing living beings, and isn't truly the one killing, extends the five-factor analysis to its most extreme test case — even the gravest action, done from selfless understanding, doesn't bind in the way ordinary agency would suggest.

sanskrit_sloka:
జ్ఞానం జ్ఞేయం పరిజ్ఞాతా త్రివిధా కర్మచోదనా ।
కరణం కర్మ కర్తేతి త్రివిధః కర్మసంగ్రహః ।। 18 ।।
translation_en: Jnana, Jnya (the object of knowledge), and the seeker of Jnana - these three induce Karma. Karana, Kriya, Karta, - these are the three limbs of Karma.
explanation_en: Naming knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower as three factors that motivate action, alongside the instrument, the act, and the agent as three components of action itself, builds out an even more granular framework — six elements total, each of which the coming verses will classify by guna.

sanskrit_sloka:
జ్ఞానం కర్మ చ కర్తా చ త్రిధైవ గుణభేదతః ।
ప్రోచ్యతే గుణసంఖ్యానే యథావఛ్చృణు తాన్యపి ।। 19 ।।
translation_en: Sankhya Shastra states that these are three types of tri-gunas of nature - knowledge, karma, and action. Listen as I tell you these differences now.
explanation_en: Announcing that knowledge, action, and the doer will each be examined according to the three gunas sets up the chapter's next major movement — having established the mechanics of action in general, Krishna now turns to categorizing the quality behind each piece of that mechanism.

sanskrit_sloka:
సర్వ భూతేశు యేనైకం భావమవ్యయమీక్షతే ।
అవిభక్తం విభక్తేషు తత్ జ్ఞానం విద్ధి సాత్వికం ।। 20 ।।
translation_en: The knowledge in sattva guna is knowing that there is one undivided, impermanent entity in all the different forms of life.
explanation_en: Sattvic knowledge is defined as perceiving a single, undivided, imperishable reality present within all the diverse forms of life — unity underneath apparent multiplicity, the same vision that's recurred throughout the text whenever equanimity or liberation has been described.
word_by_word_meaning_en: sarva-bhuteshu — among all living beings; yena — by what; ekam — alone; bhava — disposition; avyam — ephemeral; eksate — can be seen; avibhaktam — undivided; vibhaktesu — in diversity; tat — that; jnana — knowledge; viddhi — understand; sattvikam — as in sattva guna.

sanskrit_sloka:
పృథక్త్వేన తు యత్ జ్ఞానం నానాభావాన్ పృథగ్విధాన్ ।
వేత్తి సర్వేషు భూతేషు తత్ జ్ఞానం విద్ధి రాజసమ్ ।। 21 ।।
translation_en: Realize that any knowledge which sees the different kinds of beings in different bodies as separate and unrelated to each other is rajasika (in rajaguna).
explanation_en: Rajasic knowledge, by contrast, perceives beings as fundamentally separate and disconnected from one another based on their different forms — not wrong exactly, but partial, stopping at surface distinction without perceiving the underlying unity sattvic knowledge would reveal.

sanskrit_sloka:
యత్తు కృత్స్నవదేకస్మిన్ కార్యే సక్తమహైతుకమ్ ।
అతత్త్వార్థవదల్పం చ తత్తామసముదాహృతమ్ ।। 22 ।।
translation_en: In the case that the entire creation is made up of these different parts, it is said that the knowledge that makes man completely alien to himself, without logic and far from truth, is tamasic knowledge.
explanation_en: Tamasic knowledge clings to one small fragment as if it were the whole, without reason or grasp of actual truth — the most limited of the three, mistaking a narrow, disconnected view for complete understanding, with no larger context to correct the error.

sanskrit_sloka:
నియతం సంగరహితం అరాగద్వేషతః కృతమ్ ।
అఫలప్రేప్సునా కర్మ యత్తత్ సాత్త్వికముచ్యతే ।। 23 ।।
translation_en: That which is done according to karma-sastra, is free from lust, and is done without desire for fruit, is said to be in sattva guna.
explanation_en: Sattvic action is defined as prescribed duty, performed without attachment, free from desire for its fruit — the same qualifiers that have shaped the definition of sattvic renunciation and sacrifice throughout the chapter now apply equally to the general category of action itself.

sanskrit_sloka:
యత్తు కామేప్సునా కర్మ సాహంకారేణ వా పునః ।
క్రియతే బహుళాయాసం తద్రాజసముదాహృతమ్ ।। 24 ।।
translation_en: Work motivated by selfish desire, carried out by pride, and involving intense effort is said to be in Rajoguna.
explanation_en: Rajasic action is driven by personal desire, performed with considerable ego-involvement and strain — the effort here isn't neutral; it's charged with self-interest and exertion, distinguishing it clearly from the calmer, duty-oriented sattvic version.

sanskrit_sloka:
అనుబంధం క్షయం హింసామనపేక్ష్య చ పౌరుషమ్ ।
మోహాదారభ్యతే కర్మ యత్తత్తామసముచ్యతే ।। 25 ।।
translation_en: Karma that one does, starting from delusion, without knowing what one's self-power is, and without thinking about the consequences, loss and harm to others - is called Tamasika Karma.
explanation_en: Tamasic action arises from delusion, undertaken without regard for one's actual capacity or for the consequences and harm it might cause others — recklessness rather than malice necessarily, but recklessness with real potential for damage, born of simply not thinking clearly.

sanskrit_sloka:
ముక్త సంగోఽనహంవాదీ ధృత్యుత్సాహసమన్వితః ।
సిద్ద్యసిద్ధ్యోర్నిర్వికారః కర్తా సాత్విక ఉచ్యతే ।। 26 ।।
translation_en: Those who are free from ego and association, and have enthusiasm, determination, and are indifferent to success or failure are said to be virtuous doers.
explanation_en: A sattvic doer is free from ego and attachment, works with enthusiasm and determination, and remains unmoved by success or failure — a portrait that finally brings together, in a single figure, nearly every quality this chapter and the ones before it have praised.

sanskrit_sloka:
రాగీ కర్మఫలప్రేప్సుః లుభ్ధో హింసాత్మకోఽశుచిః ।
హర్షశోకాన్వితః కర్తా రాజసః పరికీర్తితః ।। 27 ।।
translation_en: A Karta who is interested in the fruits of karma, greedy, violent-inclined, impure, and affected by Harsha-Sokamas is considered to be in Rajoguna.
explanation_en: A rajasic doer is driven by desire for reward, greedy, prone to harm others, impure, and swept along by joy and sorrow — someone capable and energetic, perhaps, but whose energy is entangled with exactly the attachments a sattvic doer has released.

sanskrit_sloka:
అయుక్తః ప్రాకృతః స్తబ్ధః శఠో నైష్కృతికోఽలసః ।
విషాదీ దీర్ఘసూత్రీ చ కర్తా తామస ఉచ్యతే ।। 28 ।।
translation_en: Those who are undisciplined, scornful, foolish, foolish, mean, lazy, desperate and carelessly waste time - may be called tamoguna kartas.
explanation_en: A tamasic doer is undisciplined, vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, lazy, despondent, and endlessly procrastinating — the least capable version, lacking not just the right motive but the basic follow-through that would let good intention translate into completed action.
word_by_word_meaning_en: ayuktah — without discipline; prakritah — vulgar; stabdhah — stupid; shatah — hypocritical; naishkritikah — dishonest (or) vile; Alasah — laziness (with laziness) ; sadhi — unhappy and angry; dirgha-sutri — one who spends time carelessly; Cha — and; karta — karta (doer); tamasah — in tamoguna; Uchyate — will be said.

sanskrit_sloka:
బుద్ధేర్భేదం ధృతేశ్చైవ గుణతస్త్రివిధం శృణు ।
ప్రోచ్యమానమశేషేణ పృథక్త్వేన ధనంజయ ।। 29 ।।
translation_en: Now listen, O Arjuna, I will explain at length the difference between the intellect and the senses according to the trigunas of nature.
explanation_en: Promising to explain the intellect and determination according to the three gunas as well signals the chapter still has more ground to cover — knowledge and action have been classified, and now the underlying mental faculties that produce them come under the same three-fold analysis.
word_by_word_meaning_en: buddheh — of the mind; bhedama — distinctions; dhruthe — of strong will; Cha — and; eva — truly; gunah trividham — according to the three modes of nature; srinu — hear; prochyamanam — described; asesana — abundantly; prithaktvena — separately; Dhanunjaya — conqueror of wealth, Arjuna.

sanskrit_sloka:
ప్రవృత్తిం చ నివృత్తిం చ కార్యాకార్యే భయాభయే ।
బంధం మోక్షం చ యా వేత్తి బుద్దిః సా పార్థ సాత్త్వికీ ।। 30 ।।
translation_en: O Partha, what is the right deed, what is the bad deed;  What is duty, what is not duty; What to fear, what not to fear; Buddhi is said to be in Sattva Guna when it is understood what is binding and what is salvation.
explanation_en: Sattvic intellect correctly distinguishes right action from wrong, duty from non-duty, fear from fearlessness, and bondage from liberation — a comprehensive clarity across every major distinction this whole text has been trying to help Arjuna make since chapter 1.
word_by_word_meaning_en: propensity — activities; Cha — and; Nirutti — ceasing operations; Cha — and; karya — prescribed actions to be performed; acarye — prohibited acts; bhaya — fear; abhaye — fearlessly; bandham — bonding factor; moksha — gives salvation; Cha — and; ya — whatever; vetti — deciphered; buddhih — intellect; sa — that; Partha — son of Pritha; sattviki — as being in sattva guna.

sanskrit_sloka:
యయా ధర్మమధర్మం చ కార్యం చాకార్యమేవ చ ।
అయథావత్ప్రజానాతి బుద్ధిః సా పార్థ రాజసీ ।। 31 ।।
translation_en: Whenever the mind is confused as to what is right and what is wrong, when it cannot know what is right behavior and what is wrong, then that mind is in Rajoguna.
explanation_en: Rajasic intellect grows confused about right and wrong, unable to reliably distinguish proper conduct from improper — not entirely blind, but unreliable, prone to getting the crucial distinctions wrong precisely when it matters most.

sanskrit_sloka:
అధర్మం ధర్మమితి యా మన్యతే తమసావృతా ।
సర్వార్థాన్విపరీతాంశ్చ బుద్ధిః సా పార్థ తామసీ ।। 32 ।।
translation_en: Tamoguna Buddhi is the mind which is enveloped in darkness and considers unrighteousness as righteousness and falsehood as truth.
explanation_en: Tamasic intellect, shrouded in darkness, mistakes unrighteousness for righteousness and falsehood for truth — a complete inversion rather than mere confusion, actively getting the fundamental categories backwards rather than simply failing to see clearly.

sanskrit_sloka:
ధృత్యా యయా ధారయతే మనఃప్రాణేంద్రియక్రియాః ।
యోగేనావ్యభిచారిణ్యా ధృతిః సా పార్థ సాత్త్వికీ ।। 33 ।।
translation_en: Strong will developed through yoga; And the will that underlies the activities of the mind, prana vayus, and senses is called sattva guna dhrdhamsakata.
explanation_en: Sattvic resolve is the steady will, developed through yogic practice, that governs the mind, life-force, and senses in unified purpose — determination here isn't stubbornness but coherent inner alignment, everything pulling in the same disciplined direction.

sanskrit_sloka:
యయా తు ధర్మకామార్థాన్ ధృత్యా ధారయతేఽర్జున ।
ప్రసంగేన ఫలాకాంక్షీ ధృతిః సా పార్థ రాజసీ ।। 34 ।।
translation_en: Rajasika dhruthi is a fixed mind motivated by desire and interested in dharma (duties), kama (pleasures) and artha (wealth).
explanation_en: Rajasic resolve is fixed on duty, pleasure, and wealth out of personal desire and attachment to results — a real determination, but one whose energy is bound to specific outcomes rather than flowing from disciplined inner unity.

sanskrit_sloka:
యయా స్వప్నం భయం శోకం విషాదం మదమేవ చ ।
న విముంచతి దుర్మేధా ధృతిః సా పార్థ తామసీ ।। 35 ।।
translation_en: Tamoguna dhruthi is the low minded will that is unrelenting, daydreaming, fearful, grieving, depressed and arrogant.
explanation_en: Tamasic resolve is the low, stubborn will clung to by someone lost in daydreaming, fear, grief, despair, and arrogance — will that persists not from strength but from an inability to release unhelpful patterns, mistaking rigidity for genuine steadiness.

sanskrit_sloka:
సుఖం త్విదానీం త్రివిధం శృణు మే భరతర్షభ ।
అభ్యాసాద్రమతే యత్ర దుఃఖాంతం చ నిగచ్ఛతి ।। 36 ।।
translation_en: And now hear from me, O Arjuna, about the three kinds of pleasures which the living soul attains, and about the attainment of the stage of liberation from all sorrows.
explanation_en: Introducing the three kinds of happiness, and the state of liberation from all sorrow, moves the analysis into one final category — after knowledge, action, the doer, intellect, and resolve, the chapter now turns to what different kinds of satisfaction actually feel like from the inside.

sanskrit_sloka:
యత్తదగ్రే విషమివ పరిణామేఽమృతోపమమ్ ।
తత్సుఖం సాత్వికం ప్రోక్తమ్ ఆత్మబుద్ధిప్రసాదజమ్ ।। 37 ।।
translation_en: Sattva guna happiness is happiness that seems like poison in the beginning, but in the end is like nectar. It is born of the pure intellect that is rooted in self-knowledge.
explanation_en: Sattvic happiness, described as bitter at first but sweet in the end, born from the clarity of self-knowledge, captures something true about disciplined effort generally — the reward isn't immediate, and the path there can feel unpleasant before its value becomes clear.

sanskrit_sloka:
విషయేంద్రియసంయోగాత్ యత్తదగ్రేఽమృతోపమమ్ ।
పరిణామే విషమివ తత్సుఖం రాజసం స్మృతమ్ ।। 38 ।।
translation_en: The pleasure due to the contact of sense objects with the senses is called rajasic (rajo guna) pleasure. This pleasure is like nectar in the beginning, but in the end it is like poison.
explanation_en: Rajasic happiness, arising from the contact of senses with their objects, is described in the exact reverse pattern — sweet at first, bitter in the end — a precise inversion that makes the contrast with sattvic happiness impossible to miss.

sanskrit_sloka:
యదగ్రే  చానుబంధే చ సుఖం మోహనమాత్మనః ।
నిద్రాలస్యప్రమాదోత్థం తత్తామసముదాహృతమ్ ।। 39 ।।
translation_en: Whatever happiness - covering the entire existence of the soul from beginning to end, and arising from sleep, laziness, and carelessness - is said to be tamasic (in tamoguna) happiness.
explanation_en: Tamasic happiness, arising from sleep, laziness, and negligence, and clouding the self from beginning to end, doesn't even carry the temporary sweetness rajasic pleasure offers — it's presented as diminished satisfaction throughout, rather than pleasure that later curdles.

sanskrit_sloka:
న తదస్తి పృథివ్యాం వా దివి దేవేషు వా పునః ।
సత్త్వం ప్రకృతిజైర్ముక్తం యదేభిః స్యాత్ త్రిభిర్గుణైః ।। 40 ।।
translation_en: In this physical world - not on earth, or in the upper heavenly worlds - not a single living being is beyond the influence of these trigunas of nature.
explanation_en: The observation that not a single being anywhere — on earth or among the celestial worlds — escapes the influence of these three gunas closes out the long classification section with a universalizing note: this entire framework applies to everyone, without exception, regardless of status or realm.

sanskrit_sloka:
బ్రాహ్మణక్షత్రియవిశాం శూద్రాణాం చ పరంతప ।
కర్మాణి ప్రవిభక్తాని స్వభావప్రభవైర్గుణైః ।। 41 ।।
translation_en: Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras – whose duties were assigned according to their characteristics, their respective qualities. (not in terms of birth).
explanation_en: Assigning duties to Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras based on their qualities rather than birth is a striking clarification — the parenthetical is doing real work, insisting this social division was never meant to be an accident of ancestry but a match to actual temperament and capacity.

sanskrit_sloka:
శమో దమస్తపః శౌచం క్షాంతిరార్జవమేవ చ ।
జ్ఞానం విజ్ఞానమాస్తిక్యం బ్రహ్మకర్మ స్వభావజమ్ ।। 42 ।।
translation_en: Sama (tranquility), dama (sensual restraint), austerity, purity, patience, sincerity, wisdom, knowledge, and faith in this world – these are the innate karmic qualities of Brahmins.
explanation_en: Listing tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, patience, integrity, wisdom, and faith as the natural qualities of the Brahmin describes a temperament oriented toward reflection and inner discipline — a description of character first, occupation second.

sanskrit_sloka:
శౌర్యం తేజో ధృతిర్దాక్ష్యం యుద్ధే చాప్యపలాయనమ్ ।
దానమీశ్వరభావశ్చ క్షాత్రం కర్మ స్వభావజమ్ ।। 43 ।।
translation_en: Valor, strength, courage, skill in arms training, determination not to back down from battle, large-hearted kindness, and leadership ability - these are the karmic qualities inherent in Kshatriyas.
explanation_en: Valor, strength, determination in battle, generosity, and leadership define the Kshatriya nature — directly relevant to Arjuna himself, given that this entire eighteen-chapter conversation began with him questioning whether his own warrior duty was justified.

sanskrit_sloka:
కృషిగౌరక్ష్యవాణిజ్యం వైశ్యకర్మస్వభావజమ్ ।
పరిచర్యాత్మకం కర్మ శూద్రస్యాపి స్వభావజమ్ ।। 44 ।।
translation_en: Agriculture, dairy farming, and trade are natural occupations for those with Vaishya Gunas. Serving by performing deeds is the natural duty of those with shudra qualities.
explanation_en: Farming, animal husbandry, and trade for the Vaishya, service through action for the Shudra — completing the four-fold picture with occupations oriented toward production, exchange, and support, each treated as equally legitimate expressions of natural aptitude.

sanskrit_sloka:
స్వే స్వే కర్మణ్యభిరతః సంసిద్ధిం లభతే నరః ।
స్వకర్మనిరతః సిద్ధిం యథా విందతి తత్ శృణు ।। 45 ।।
translation_en: By performing the duties of those who are naturally born, human beings can attain perfect siddhi. Now hear from me how one can achieve perfection by practicing/performing his assigned duties.
explanation_en: The claim that performing one's natural duty, whatever it is, leads to perfection reframes social role not as a hierarchy of worth but as a hierarchy of function — every position, done well and for the right reasons, is described as an equally viable route to the same ultimate goal.

sanskrit_sloka:
యతః ప్రవృత్తిర్భూతానాం యేన సర్వమిదం తతమ్ ।
స్వకర్మణా తమభ్యర్చ్య సిద్ధిం విందతి మానవః ।। 46 ।।
translation_en: By performing his natural occupation one worships Him - from whom all the demons sprang and by whom the whole world is filled and concentrated.  By doing such things one attains Siddhi easily.
explanation_en: Worshipping the divine source of all beings specifically through the performance of one's natural work turns ordinary occupation into a form of devotion — work itself, done rightly, becomes indistinguishable from worship rather than existing as a separate, lesser activity.

sanskrit_sloka:
శ్రేయాన్ స్వధర్మో విగుణః పరధర్మాత్ స్వనుష్ఠితాత్ ।
స్వభావనియతం కర్మ కుర్వన్నాప్నోతి కిల్బిషమ్   ।। 47 ।।
translation_en: It is better for a person to do his own self-righteousness, even if it is not done properly, than to do para (others') dharma. In performing the duties of his nature, man does not incur sin.
explanation_en: The famous claim that it's better to perform one's own duty imperfectly than another's duty well returns to a principle first raised back in chapter 3 — authenticity in one's own role outweighs competence borrowed from someone else's, a point important enough to restate near the very end.
word_by_word_meaning_en: sreyan — excellent; svadharmaḥ — his own prescribed vocation dharmas; vigunah — even if not done properly; para-dharmat — the dharmas of others;  su-anushthitat — well done; svabhava-niatam — according to one's nature; karma — duty; kurvan — by doing; na-apnoti — does not get; Kilbisham — sin.

sanskrit_sloka:
సహజం కర్మ కౌంతేయ సదోషమపి న త్యజేత్ ।
సర్వారంభా హి దోషేణ ధూమేనాగ్నిరివావృతాః  ।। 48 ।।
translation_en: One should never forsake the duties born of one's natural nature, even if there are faults in them, O son of Kunti. All karmic efforts are shrouded in some kind of dosha, just as a fire is shrouded in smoke.
explanation_en: The comparison of all action to fire wrapped in smoke — inherently imperfect, yet not something to abandon on that account — offers real reassurance: the presence of flaws in one's work isn't grounds for giving it up, since flawlessness was never actually available to begin with.
